It was during his reign, a temple dedicated to Surya was constructed by the silk-weavers at Dashpur. The temple was renovated by the same guild.

23.s: Which of the following inscriptions is known as the first advertisement of the World?
23.x: Dashpur inscription is the first advertisement of the world. Also known as Mandsaur inscription, it belongs to the period of Kumargupta-I and contains advertisements about silk trade.

23.s: What did some Gupta-period guilds maintain for their protection?
23.x: Some guilds had their own armed bodies (APPSC 2023 key); guild charity built temples, rest houses, halls and gardens.
xa: Guilds framed their **own rules**, had **executive committees/heads** and **their own seals**.
They received **public deposits** and gave loans.
⚠ "**Non-autonomous bodies**" is always the wrong option on guild features (APPSC 2022, 2023).
Gupta and Vakataka **seals** name artisans, merchants and guilds.

23.s: In the Gupta period, what was the head of a guild called?
23.x: The head of a guild was the Sreshthi or Setti; a Sarthavaha was a caravan trader in long-distance trade.
xa: **Shreni** = guild.
In the town council the **Sarthavaha** sat beside the **nagarashreshthi**, **prathama kulika** and **prathama kayastha** (Damodarpur plates).
**Damodarpur copper plates** show guilds acting as **banks**.
Guilds settled internal disputes and regulated trade.

23.s: The Indore copper plate records an endowment with which guild for maintaining a temple lamp?
23.x: The Indore plate concerns the oil-men's guild and a temple lamp; the Dashpur inscription concerns the silk-weavers' guild and the Damodarpur plates guild banking.
xa: Mandsaur = **world's first advertisement**, composed by **Vatsabhatti**.
Indore plate: guild of oil-men of **Indrapura**, under **Skandagupta**.
Damodarpur plates belong to **Kumaragupta I**.

23.s: Which Gupta records show guilds acting as banks?
23.x: The Damodarpur copper plates of Kumaragupta I show guilds acting as banks; the Indore plate records the oil-men's lamp endowment.

23.s: From where did the silk-weavers' guild of the Mandsaur (Dashpur) inscription migrate to Dashpur?
23.x: The guild came from Lata in Gujarat and built a Sun temple at Dashpur; weavers changing profession point to falling silk demand.
xa: Temple built **436–37 CE**, repaired **473 CE**.
Composed by **Vatsabhatti**, not Bhava.
Called the **oldest advertisement** in Indian tradition.

23.s: Who composed the Dashpur (Mandsaur) inscription, called the oldest advertisement in the Indian tradition?
23.x: The Dashpur inscription was composed by Vatsabhatti, not Bhava (the MPPSC trap).
xa: It records a **silk weavers' guild** from **Lata (Gujarat)** that migrated to Dashpur and built a **Sun temple**.
It dates to **Kumaragupta I** and **Bandhuvarman**; the repair is dated **473 CE**.
Several weavers changed professions — a sign of **falling silk demand**.
⚠ **Indore** plate = oil-men + lamp; **Damodarpur** = guild banks + town council.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about guilds in the Gupta period?
o: They received public deposits and gave loans
They framed their own rules and used their own seals
Some of them kept their own armed bodies
They were controlled by royal officials and had no autonomy
23.x: Gupta guilds were autonomous bodies with their own rules, seals, banking work and sometimes armed bodies.

23.s: The Indore copper plate, recording an endowment with the guild of oil-men, belongs to the reign of which Gupta ruler?
23.x: The Indore copper plate of Skandagupta records an endowment with the oil-men of Indrapura to keep a lamp burning in a Sun temple.

23.s: Which one of the following ports handled the North Indian trade during the Gupta period?
23.x: Tamralipti (modern Tamluk in West Bengal) was the principal port that handled the trade of northern India during the Gupta period.

23.s: With reference to the period of the Gupta dynasty in ancient India, the towns Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were well known as
o: places of exquisite stone art and architecture.
23.x: Prominent sea ports of the Gupta era included Tamralipti, Arikamedu, Muziris, Sopara, Chaul (23 miles to the south of Mumbai, West coast), Kadura, and Kontakossylla (Ghantasala, Andhra coast), all of which were well connected via inland routes across the Gupta Empire.

23.s: With reference to the period of Gupta dynasty in ancient India, the towns Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were well known as
o: places of exquisite stone art and architecture
23.x: During Gupta period there was flourishing external and internal trade. Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were ports handling foreign trade.

23.s: Which one of the following ports was in use for the North Indian trade during the Gupta period?
23.x: Tamralipti, on the east coast, was the port that handled North Indian trade in the Gupta period, while Broach, Kalyan and Cambay were western ports.

23.s: Which one of the following ports handled the North Indian trade during the Gupta period ?
23.x: The Tamralipti port in Bengal was a prominent port during the Gupta period from where trade was conducted with South-East Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra as well as northern India. Western coast had an important port of Bhrigu Kachchha (Bharuch) from where Gupta rulers used to trade with western countries.

23.s: Where were Ghantasala and Kadura, ports of the Gupta period, located?
23.x: Ghantasala and Kadura were in Krishna district, while Kalyan and Chaul were on the Konkan coast.
xa: ⚠ **Kalyan** is in Maharashtra, not Karnataka.
UPSC **2020**: Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul handled **foreign trade**.
**Motupalli and Koduru** served Southeast Asian trade under the **Vishnukundins**.

23.s: Which was the largest west-coast port in the Gupta period?
23.x: Bharuch was the largest west-coast port; Tamralipti was an eastern port and Ghantasala and Kadura were in Krishna district.
xa: **Bharuch** = Gujarat, largest west-coast port.
**Ghantasala** = Kantakasela.
Main import: **silk from China**.

23.s: Where did Sopara, a major Gupta-era centre of trade with Rome and South-East Asia, lie?
23.x: Sopara and Barbaricum were in western India; Pratishthana lay in the Deccan.
xa: The Bengal port was **Tamralipti** (Tamluk).
**Kalyan** and **Chaul** were on the **Maharashtra (Konkan)** coast.
**Ghantasala (Kantakasela)** and **Kadura** were in Krishna district, **Andhra**.
Deccan route: **Ujjain-Bharuch via Paithan and Tagara**, **Paithan-Sopara**.

23.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Tamralipti – Western port at the mouth of the Narmada
Bharuch – Eastern port at the mouth of the Kaveri
23.x: Tamralipti was the eastern port in Bengal; Bhrigukachchha (Bharuch) was the western port at the mouth of the Narmada.
n: Tamralipti was associated with Gupta international trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 99-100]
Bhrigukachchha is also known as Bharuch. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 99-100]
Bhrigukachchha was associated with Western trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 99-100]
xa: Bharuch is also called **Barygaza / Broach** — the largest west-coast port (APP).
Andhra ports: **Ghantasala** and **Kadura** (Krishna district).
UPSC 2020: **Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul** handled foreign trade in the Gupta period.
⚠ **Kalyan** = Maharashtra, not Karnataka.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ancient South Indian trade centres?
o: Arikamedu had no part in international trade
Kaveripattanam lay at the mouth of the Kaveri
23.x: Arikamedu, like Kaveripattanam, was a centre of international trade, including trade with Rome.
n: Arikamedu was located in South India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Arikamedu belonged to the Gupta-era trade network. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Arikamedu was associated with international trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Arikamedu was a major centre of international trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Kaveripattanam was located in South India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Kaveripattanam belonged to the Gupta-era trade network. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Kaveripattanam was associated with international trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]
Kaveripattanam was a major centre of international trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 64-67]

23.s: On which coast did the Gupta-period ports Kalyan and Chaul lie?
23.x: Kalyan and Chaul were on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, not Karnataka.

23.s: At the mouth of which river did Bhrigukachchha (Bharuch), the largest west-coast port, lie?
23.x: Bharuch (Broach, Barygaza) lay at the mouth of the Narmada in Gujarat.

23.s: Where was the port of Tamralipti located?
23.x: Tamralipti (Tamluk) in Bengal was the chief port for North Indian trade with South-East Asia.

23.s: Under which Andhra dynasty did the ports of Motupalli and Koduru serve trade with South-East Asia?
23.x: Motupalli and Koduru served South-East Asian trade under the Vishnukundins.

23.s: By which name was Ghantasala, a port in Krishna district, known to classical writers?
23.x: Ghantasala was Kontakossylla; Kadura was Koddura.

23.s: Of which metal was the Gupta rupaka made?
23.x: The rupaka was a silver coin issued after the conquest of the Western Satraps; gold dinaras were issued in the largest numbers.
xa: **Cowries** were used for small daily exchange (noted by **Fa-Hien**).
Gold content of dinaras **fell** in later reigns — **debasement**.
Copper coin names in glossaries: **kakini, karshapana**.
Gold coins became scarce after the Guptas.

23.s: In Gupta times, with what was ordinary daily exchange mainly carried on?
23.x: Cowries were used in ordinary exchange; copper issues were few and later dinaras contained less gold.
xa: Gold dinaras were issued in the **largest numbers**.
Silver **rupaka** came after conquering the **Western Satraps**.
R.S. Sharma links **scarce gold coins** to **urban decay**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements about Gupta coinage:
1. Gold dinaras were issued in the largest numbers.
2. Later dinaras contained less gold and more alloy.
3. Silver rupakas were issued after the defeat of the Kushanas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
23.x: Dinaras were the most numerous and declined in purity; rupakas followed the defeat of the Western Satraps, not the Kushanas.

23.s:
Identify the correct sentences regarding the economic conditions of the Sangam age.

a. Madurai was famous for cotton trade.

b. Sea pearls and Precious stones were the main exports.

c. Tamils traded with Egypt and Arabia.

d. Decline of trade was one of the causes for the decay of the Tamil Kingdoms.

23.s: The decline of trade and commerce in North India between 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the
o: Decline in skills of Indian artisans

23.s: The gradual decline of towns was an important feature of which period?
23.x: During the Gupta period, towns declined gradually. Most of the towns that were prosperous in the valley, declined in that age. A major city, Pataliputra became a village when Hiuen-Tsang came to India. Mathura, Sonpur, Hastinapur, Sravasti etc., all major cities provided evidence of a decline in this age. So, we can say that the gradual decline of towns is an important feature of the Gupta period.

23.s: From the third century AD when the Huna invasion ended the Roman Empire, the Indian merchants relied more and more on the :
23.x: When the Huna invasion ended the Roman empire in 3rd century A.D. the Indian merchants relied more and more on the South East Asian trade.

23.s: Vishti and feudal obligations on peasants form the basis of which interpretation of the Gupta economy?
23.x: Peasant obligations, including vishti or forced labour, form the basis of the urban decay and feudalism critique of the Gupta economy.
xa: **Vishti** = forced labour.
Declining towns: **Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti, Kaushambi**.
**c. 750–1000 CE** = stagnation in North India.

23.s: The decline in Indian silk exports to the Eastern Roman Empire was principally associated with which development?
o: The Sassanids prohibited the silk trade.
The Gupta rulers banned the export of silk.
The Romans learnt to rear silkworms.
23.x: Indian silk exports suffered after the Romans learnt to rear silkworms themselves.
23.tq: Identify the cause directly linked to the decline rather than a nearby political event.
xs: Silk exports to the **Eastern Roman Empire** fell once **the Romans learnt to rear silkworms** — option **(4)**.
That trade continued until about **550 CE**.
xa: **Collapse of the West Roman Empire** = standard cause (APPSC-G2 **2017** key).
**Sassanid** decline after the rise of Islam hurt overland trade.
Trade shifted to **South-East Asia** via **Tamralipti**.

23.s: The decline of trade in North India after the Guptas reduced the inflow of which of the following?
23.x: Losing the north-western route and western India cut trade revenue and the inflow of gold and silver.
xa: **Eastern Roman** silk and spice trade lasted until about **550 CE**, until the Romans learnt to **rear silkworms**.
**Collapse of the West Roman Empire** = standard cause of North India's trade decline (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
Decaying towns: **Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti, Kaushambi** (APPSC-GS 2023 key).
c. **750-1000 CE** = stagnation in North India.

23.s: In Gupta-period sources, what does 'Chinansuka' refer to?
23.x: Chinansuka means Chinese silk and shows the growth of trade with China.
xa: **Sassanid decline** after the rise of Islam hurt overland trade.
**R.S. Sharma**: old commercial towns shrank and the economy turned rural and self-sufficient.
⚠ "Decline pronounced only by the mid-9th century" was marked **false**.
Decline was visible in the **post-Gupta period / 7th century**.

23.s: With which historian is the 'urban decay' interpretation of the post-Gupta period associated?
23.x: R.S. Sharma's urban decay thesis links shrinking towns, rural self-sufficiency and scarce gold coins.
xa: Declining towns: **Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti, Kaushambi** (APPSC-GS **2023**).
Peasants bore **vishti** + feudal obligations — basis of the **urban decay / feudalism** critique.
Later dinaras were **debased** — less gold, more alloy.

23.s: Until about which year did Indian trade with the Eastern Roman Empire continue?
23.x: Eastern Roman trade continued until about 550 CE, before the post-Gupta decline and the stagnation of c. 750-1000 CE.
xa: **West Roman collapse** = standard cause of trade decline (APPSC-G2 **2017** key).
**Sassanid decline** after the rise of Islam hurt overland trade.
**Hunas** disrupted the north-western route.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about urban decay after the Guptas?
o: Pataliputra had become a village when Hiuen-Tsang came
Sanghol and Hastinapur were among the declining towns
Stagnation lasted from about 750 to 1000 CE
Towns declined only by the mid-9th century
23.x: Gradual decline of towns was already a feature of the Gupta period and visible in the 7th century.

23.s: The decline of which empire after the rise of Islam hurt India's overland trade?
23.x: The Sassanid decline after the rise of Islam hurt overland trade.

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. After the fall of Rome, Indian merchants relied more on South-East Asian trade through Tamralipti.
2. The shift to South-East Asian trade revived the economy of North India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
23.x: Merchants turned to South-East Asian trade via Tamralipti after Rome fell, but this did not revive the northern economy.

23.s: Which invaders blocked the north-western trade route of India in the late Gupta period?
23.x: The Hunas blocked the north-western route, and the loss of western India cut the inflow of gold and silver.

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ghantasala and Kadura were east-coast ports of Andhra.
2. The Satavahana weavers' guild was called Kolika Shreni.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
23.x: Ghantasala and Kadura in Krishna district were Andhra's east-coast ports, and the Satavahana weavers' guild was Kolika Shreni.
xa: Both ports are in **Krishna district**; Kadura is near **Gudur**.
**Motupalli and Koduru** served Southeast Asian trade under the **Vishnukundins**.
**Shreni** = guild; head = **Sreshthi / Setti**.

24.s: Which one of the following best describes a major religious change during the Gupta period?
o: Temple worship was replaced entirely by Vedic fire sacrifices.
Idol worship was prohibited in public temples.
Theistic and devotional Hinduism increasingly replaced sacrificial Brahmanism.
Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh ceased to be regarded as supreme deities.
24.x: Hinduism became increasingly theistic and devotional, while temple-based idol worship became common and the earlier dominance of sacrificial Brahmanism declined.
24.tq: Choose the comprehensive description of a religious transition.
xs: **Theistic and devotional** religion replaced **sacrificial Brahmanism** — option **(3)**.
**Idol worship in temples** became common — shift from Vedic fire altar to temple.
**Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh** were the supreme deities.
xa: Comparative: Mauryan = **Vedic + Shramana**; Gupta = **sacrifice → temple and bhakti**.
**Smarta** practices spread.
**Six schools** of philosophy took final shape.

24.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Moksha — one of the three components of Trivarga
24.x: The four Purusharthas are Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha. The first three together are called Trivarga.
24.tq: Separate the threefold Trivarga from the complete fourfold Purushartha scheme.
xs: **Trivarga = Dharma, Artha, Kama** — option **(2)**.
The four **Purusharthas** are Dharma, Artha, Kama, **Moksha**; Moksha is **not** in trivarga.
xa: Supreme deities: **Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh**.
**Smarta** practices spread.
**Six schools** of philosophy took final shape.

24.s: What are the first three Purusharthas - Dharma, Artha and Kama - together called?
24.x: Dharma, Artha and Kama form the trivarga; Moksha is the fourth Purushartha.

24.s: Which of the following was not related to the architecture of the Gupta Period?
o: Large number of Buddha images unearthed at Saranath and Banaras.
The images of Siva and Vishnu are sculptured on the walls of Deogarh Temple.
A copper image of Buddha at Nalanda.
The Besnagar Pillar which was dedicated as Garudadhvaja.

24.s: Who were the first to worship Vasudeva Krishna :
24.x: Under the Bhagavata religion, the initial form of Vaishnavism is shown in the worship of Lord Krishna, the son of Devaki. The initial name of Krishna was prevalent in the Panini age. The worshippers of Vasudev were known as Vasudevak (Bhagavata) in that age. According to Indian belief, Lord Krishna is considered as a supreme personality and has been worshipped since ancient ages.

24.s: Who contributes the most in the development of Bhagavata sect?
24.x: The Bhagavata or Vaishnava religion reached its peak in the reign of Gupta kings. Gupta kings were followers of the Vaishnava religion, and they made it a religion of the state. Most of the Gupta rulers held the title of ‘Parambhagavata.’ Garuda, the mount (Vahana) of Lord Vishnu was the state symbol of Guptas.

24.s: The earliest known epigraphic evidence of Bhagvatism is :
Which incarnation of Vishnu is depicted as saving the Earth from the Sea?
24.x: Lord Vishnu took the form of Varaha to kill the king of Giants, Hiranyaksha and released the Earth from his clutch. In the pictures of the Purana, God Varaha has been shown balancing the earth on his teeth and arising from the sea. In this incarnation, the head of Varaha is on the human body having four arms holding Shankha, Chakra, Gada and Padma in his hands like God Vishnu fighting with demon Hiranyaksha.

24.s: The originator of Bhagavata Religion was –
24.x: Traditionally, the originator of the Bhagavata religion was Vrishni (Satvat) descendant, Lord Krishna who is also known as Vasudeva. He was basically from Mathura. He has been described as the son of Devaki and the disciple of Ghor Angirasa in the Chhandogya Upanishad.

24.s: Bhagavatism centred on the worship of Vasudeva-Krishna of which clan?
24.x: Bhagavatism centred on Vasudeva-Krishna of the Vrishni (Satvata) clan; its foundations were karma, bhakti and ahimsa.
xa: It preached the **Avatara** theory of Vishnu (ten incarnations).
**Heliodorus**, envoy of Indo-Greek king **Antialcidas**, set up the **Garuda pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha)** and called himself a **Bhagavata**.
**Panini** refers to Vasudeva worship.
⚠ First **'Parama Bhagavata'**: many notes = **Chandragupta II**; UPPSC keys (2009, 2015) = **Samudragupta**.

24.s: Heliodorus, who set up the Garuda pillar at Besnagar, was the envoy of which Indo-Greek king?
24.x: Heliodorus, envoy of Antialcidas at the court of the Sunga ruler Bhagabhadra, set up the Garuda pillar to Vasudeva.
xa: **Garuda** was later the Gupta **dynastic emblem**.
The **Bhagavatas** first worshipped Vasudeva-Krishna (UPPSC **1997**).
**Panini** refers to Vasudeva worship.

24.s: Gupta-period Vaishnavism preached the theory of how many incarnations of Vishnu?
24.x: The avatara theory of ten incarnations of Vishnu was preached during the Gupta period.
xa: Colossal **Varaha** panel at **Udayagiri** under **Chandragupta II**.
Vaishnava symbols: **chakra, shankha, Garuda**; centre **Mathura**.
Text: **Bhagavad Gita**.

24.s: Under whose patronage was the colossal Varaha panel at Udayagiri carved?
24.x: The colossal Varaha panel at Udayagiri was carved under Chandragupta II, and the cave functioned as his personal temple.
xs: The colossal **Varaha** panel at **Udayagiri** was carved under **Chandragupta II** — option **(1)**.
The cave was his **personal temple**.
xa: It is read as his **rescue of the land**, e.g. from the **Sakas**.
Udayagiri (MP) has **1 Jain cave** among **20**.
**Udayagiri Cave 4** holds an **Ekamukhalinga**.

24.s: The Gupta kings, who called themselves 'Parambhagavata', used which emblem?
24.x: The Gupta kings called themselves Parambhagavata and used the Garuda emblem, marking them as Vaishnavas.
n: The Guptas were associated with Vaishnavism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Guptas were called Parambhagavatas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Guptas used Garuda symbolism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: **Vaishnavism** developed from the **Bhagavata religion**.
The **Besnagar Garuda Pillar** of **Heliodorus** is associated with the Bhagavata religion.
**Skandagupta**'s coins carry the **Garuda standard**.
Colossal **Varaha (boar) Vishnu** panel at **Udayagiri** was carved under **Chandragupta II**.

24.s: Nandivarman II's Pedavegi inscription is regarded as the first inscription in Andhra Pradesh relating to which of the following?
24.x: The Pedavegi inscription of Nandivarman II is regarded as the first inscription in Andhra Pradesh concerning Vishnu temples.
xa: Salankayanas also used Shaiva **Parama Mahesvara** titles.
**Gudimallam's Parasurameswara** temple = oldest Shiva linga (APPSC G2 **2008**).
**Kapalikas**: **Bhairavakonda** caves.

24.s: Who is associated with the foundation of Nalanda during the Gupta period?
24.x: Kumaragupta I, also known as Shakraditya, is credited with founding Nalanda.
24.tq: Use the founder–institution trap among Gupta rulers and Buddhist centres.
xs: **Kumaragupta I (Shakraditya)** founded **Nalanda** — option **(3)**.
**Mihirakula**, the Huna, **persecuted** Buddhism.
xa: **Mahayana** images flourished in Gupta art.
Buddhism **lost royal patronage and declined**.
Buddhist centres: **Nalanda, Sarnath**.

24.s: The Vaishnava Salankayana rulers also used which Shaiva title?
24.x: The Salankayanas followed Vaishnavism, but their rulers also used Shaiva titles such as Parama Mahesvara.
xa: **Nandivarman II's Pedavegi** inscription = first in AP on **Vishnu temples**.
**Gudimallam** = oldest Shiva linga in AP.
**Kalamukha** and **Pashupata** flourished under the **Kakatiyas**.

24.s: Which Gupta ruler was the first to take the title 'Parama Bhagavata'?
24.x: Samudragupta was the first Gupta to take the title Parama Bhagavata; Chandragupta II's coins also carry it.

24.s: In which form does the colossal Udayagiri panel of Chandragupta II's time show Vishnu?
24.x: The Udayagiri panel shows Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu, in Chandragupta II's personal cave temple.

24.s: Who were the first worshippers of Vasudeva-Krishna?
24.x: The Bhagavatas (Vasudevakas) were the first worshippers of Vasudeva-Krishna; Vaishnavism grew from them.

24.s: Which is the earliest epigraphic evidence of Bhagavatism?
24.x: The Garuda pillar of Heliodorus at Besnagar (Vidisha) is the earliest epigraphic evidence of Bhagavatism.

24.s: At the court of which Sunga king did Heliodorus, who set up the Besnagar Garuda pillar, serve as envoy?
24.x: Heliodorus, envoy of Antialcidas, was at the court of the Sunga king Bhagabhadra.

24.s: With which religion is Kalika Purana associated ?
24.x: The Kalika Purana also called the Kali Purana or Sati Purana is one of the main upapurana in the Shaktism tradition of Hinduism. The text was likely composed in the Assam region of India. The text is attributed to sage Markendeya and starts off with the legends of Devi trying to bring Shiva back from ascetic life into householder's life by making him fall in love again.

24.s: How many Mahapuranas are traditionally recognised, the corpus that took its final shape in the Gupta period?
24.x: There are 18 Mahapuranas (APPSC G2 2011 key), among them Vishnu, Bhagavata, Matsya, Vayu, Brahmanda, Markandeya, Shiva and Kurma. 12, 16 and 24 are wrong; 12 is the number of land types in the Amarakosha.
xs: There are **18 Mahapuranas** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G2 **2011** key).
⚠ **12** is the number of land types in the **Amarakosha** (another topic) — not here.
xa: Principal: **Vishnu, Bhagavata, Matsya, Vayu, Brahmanda, Markandeya, Shiva, Kurma**.
Final shape in the **Gupta period** (c. 4th–6th c. CE).
Five topics: creation, re-creation, genealogies, **manvantaras**, dynastic history.

24.s: The five traditional subjects of the Puranas include which of the following?
o: Trade, taxation, diplomacy, warfare and agriculture
Creation, re-creation, genealogies, manvantaras and dynastic history

Ajanta Cave Paintings are among the oldest surviving murals in the Indian sub-continent. The Ajanta Caves were carved from volcanic rock between the 2 nd century BC and the 5 th century AD. The complex comprises around 30 caves, including unfinished ones, of which five (Caves 9, 10, 19, 26, and 29) are chaityagrihas (prayer halls), while the rest serve as viharas (monasteries). Of these, 5 caves are associated with Hinayana Buddhism, while the remaining 25 are associated with the Mahayana tradition. The paintings in the caves were first outlined in red and then filled with other colours, depicting themes primarily from Jataka tales along with references to Chinese travellers such as Faxian and Xuanzang. The artwork follows the fresco technique, in which pigments are applied to freshly laid, damp lime plaster, allowing the colours to bond firmly with the surface and remain vibrant over time. The Ajanta Caves were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. 27.s: Who was the poet in the period of The King Harshvardhan (606-647 CE)?
With reference to the history of ancient India, Bhavabhuti, Hastimalla and Kshemeshvara were famous
27.x: Bhavabhuti was an eminent playwright and poet of the 8 th century CE, regarded as one of the greatest figures in Sanskrit drama. His celebrated works—Malatimadhava, Mahaviracharita, and Uttararamacharita—are often considered comparable to Kalidasa's. Known as the "Poet of Karuna Rasa," he is believed to have served as the court poet of King Yashovarman. In the later period of regional states (c. 800–1200 CE), playwrights such as Kshemeshvara and Hastimalla gained prominence. While earlier plays, such as those of Bhavabhuti, focused on subtle dramatic elements and emotional depth, the works of Kshemeshvara, Hastimalla, and their contemporaries like Murari and Rajashekhara emphasised sophisticated poetic and linguistic techniques. This shift highlighted a literary culture that valued reading and textual appreciation over theatrical presentation (Romila Thapar, A History of India).

Consider the following about the King “Pravarasena” :

(B) His empire extended from Bundelkhand in north to Hyderabad in South.

o: More than one of the above
27.x: The Vakataka dynasty was an ancient Indian royal dynasty that ruled over the central and southern parts of India from the 3rd century CE to the end of the 5th century and the beginning of the 6th century CE. The founder of this dynasty was Vindhyashakti, whose successor was Pravarasena I, who is also considered the actual founder of the Vakataka dynasty. During the time of Pravarasena I, the boundaries of the Vakataka dynasty reached from Bundelkhand in north to Deccan (including modern Hyderabad) in the south. The Vakataka rulers expanded their territory to include vast regions under their influence. Among the rulers of the Vakataka dynasty, Pravarasena I assumed the title of Samrat (Emperor) and performed several Ashvamedha Yajnas (horse sacrifices) and Vedic rituals. According to the Puranas, he is referred to as Pravira. Thus, all the given statements are correct.

Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry) was developed as an important capital by the Eastern Chalukyas, particularly during the reign of Rajaraja Narendra. This inscription is therefore an important source for understanding the collaborative efforts behind the earliest Telugu Mahabharata and the literary patronage extended by the Eastern Chalukya rulers. The expeditions led to the conquest of Kadaram and several other places in the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. He also led the expedition up to the Godavari River and sent a victorious expedition to north India. The Chola army crossed the Ganges by defeating a number of rulers on its way. He also constructed the famous Shiva temple in that city. Rajendra Chola also conquered southern Sri Lanka, effectively bringing the entire island under Chola rule during his reign. 30.s: Which of the following gives information about local self-government during the Chola period?

31.s: Which of the following correctly describes the vimana of the Gangaikondacholapuram Temple?
o: It is 216 feet high and has a straight, rigid profile.

31.s: With which temple is the Chit Sabha, with carvings of 108 classical dance poses, associated?

31.s: Who built the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram?

Gangaikondacholapuram is associated with Rajendra I. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #148 · pp 257-259]
The Airavatesvara Temple is associated with Rajaraja II. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #148 · pp 257-259]

xa: All three temples form the UNESCO **"Great Living Chola Temples"** (Thanjavur **1987**, extended **2004**).

31.x: The Koranganatha temple at Srinivasanallur is an early Chola structural temple.

31.s: Bronze icons of Nataraja cast during the Chola period invariably show the deity with
31.x: Indian Art and Culture PMF IAS IH – 209 Chola bronze sculptures of Nataraja depict Shiva in the cosmic dance pose (Ananda Tandava) with four hands — holding the damaru (drum), agni (fire), one in abhaya mudra, and one pointing to the raised foot symbolising liberation.

31.s: Which one of the following is considered to be the world’s greatest iconographical creation made by sthapatis of South India, particularly during the Chola period?

With reference to the statue of 'Nataraja the Lord of Dance', which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The image represents dancing Shiva having four hands.
2. In his right ear, he wears a man's earring, a woman's in the left.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
31.x: The Nataraja statue of Lord Shiva represents dancing Shiva with four hands. In a single idol it depicts Shiva's role as creator, preserver and destroyer of universe. Shiva's dance is set within a halo. The god holds the damru (drum that made the first sound of creation) in his upper right hand. His upper left hand holds agni (the fire that will destroy the universe). With his lower right hand he makes abhayamudra. Shiva's front left hand, pointing to his raised left foot, signifies refuge for the troubled soul. In his right ear he wears a man's earring, a woman's in the left as a symbol of Ardhanarishwara.

31.s: Preparation of the multi-armed Nataraja by the 'Cire Perdue' (lost-wax) technique is an ancient technology of whose time?
What does the lower right hand in abhaya mudra signify in the Chola Nataraja bronze?
31.x: Abhaya mudra means 'fear not', i.e. protection; the standard Nataraja is four-armed and the lower left hand points to the raised left foot.
xa: The lower left hand gesture is **gaja-hasta**, meaning release or **liberation / refuge**.
Upper right hand: **damaru** (creation); upper left hand: **agni** (destruction).
Trampling **Apasmara** = conquest of **ignorance**.

31.s: What do the man's earring in the right ear and the woman's earring in the left ear of the Chola Nataraja symbolise?
o: the fusion of male and female principles
31.x: The different earrings of the Nataraja image represent the fusion of male and female principles.

The ring of flames, the **Prabhamandala**, stands for the cosmic cycle.
The **damaru** = creation; **agni** = destruction.

31.s: What does the damaru held in the upper right hand of the Nataraja image symbolise?
31.x: The damaru symbolises creation, the agni in the upper left hand destruction, and the prabhamandala the cosmic cycle; Apasmara represents ignorance.
xa: The standard form is **four-armed**.
**Abhaya mudra** = "fear not", i.e. protection.
The two different earrings show the fusion of **male and female** principles.

xa: Chola bronzes were **worshipped icons**.

Nataraja is **four-armed** in the standard form (**UPPSC 2021**).

31.s: What does the dwarf Apasmara under the right foot of the Chola Nataraja symbolise?
31.x: Apasmara stands for ignorance; the damaru is creation, agni destruction and abhaya protection.

31.s: What does the agni (fire) in the upper left hand of the Nataraja image symbolise?
31.x: Agni in the upper left hand stands for destruction; the damaru in the upper right stands for creation.

31.s: What do the paintings in the dark ambulatory passage of the Brihadeeswara temple depict?

Shiva as Tripurantaka and portraits of Rajaraja I with Karuvur Thevar

The coronation of Kulottunga II by Ottakuthar

31.s: Who is the guru shown with Rajaraja I in the Brihadeeswara frescoes?
31.x: The frescoes of the dark ambulatory show Rajaraja I with his guru Karuvur Thevar.

31.s: The colleges at Ennayiram and Tribhuvani (near Pondicherry) in South Arcot district were famous during which period?

31.s: Why are Rajaraja I's inscriptions at the Thanjavur temple significant?
o: The election of village assemblies through the Kudavolai system
Only the names of foreign merchants visiting the Chola ports
About 400 temple dancing women, musicians and temple staff supported by grants
The complete list of Nayanar hymns in the Tirumurai

xs: The **Uttiramerur** inscriptions of **Parantaka I** record the **Kudavolai** (pot-ballot) system of village assembly elections, so option **(2)** is correct.

31.s: At which places do Chola inscriptions record temple Vedic colleges?
31.x: Chola inscriptions record Vedic colleges at Ennayiram and Tribhuvani (near Pondicherry).

31.x: Ramavataram or Tamil Ramayanam was authored by Kamban.

31.s: Who compiled the Saiva canon Tirumurai in the time of Rajaraja I?
31.x: Nambi Andar Nambi compiled the Tirumurai, the 12-book Saiva canon of Nayanar hymns (Periya Puranam the 12th); it does not include the Vaishnava Alvar hymns.

88.s: Kakatiyas were feudatories of which Andhra dynasty?

The early Kakatiyas served as feudatories of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi before emerging as an independent power. The earliest Kakatiya chiefs such as Beta I and Prola I acknowledged the overlordship of the Eastern Chalukya rulers. As the power of the Eastern Chalukyas declined, the Kakatiyas gradually strengthened their position and eventually established an independent kingdom under Rudradeva with Warangal (Orugallu) as their capital. 88.s: To whom were the Kakatiyas feudatories before establishing their independent kingdom?

Thus, the Kakatiyas rose gradually from feudatories to one of the greatest dynasties of medieval Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

Recherla Rudra was one of the most distinguished military commanders of the Kakatiya kingdom. Who built the lake Kesari Samudra?
88.x:
Kesari Samudram is a historic irrigation tank constructed during the Kakatiya period by Rudradeva, one of the earliest powerful rulers of the Kakatiya dynasty. The Kakatiyas were renowned for their emphasis on irrigation development. They built hundreds of tanks and reservoirs to conserve rainwater and support agriculture in the dry regions of Telangana. Kesari Samudram is one such engineering achievement that contributed significantly to agricultural prosperity. The Kakatiya rulers considered irrigation as the backbone of their economy, and their tankbuilding tradition continues to benefit the region even today. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

• Builder – Rudradeva
• Dynasty – Kakatiya
• Importance – Irrigation Tank

91.s: Which dynasty built the Thousand Pillar Temple?
91.x:
The Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda is one of the finest architectural achievements of the Kakatiya dynasty. It was constructed during the reign of Rudradeva in 1163 CE. The temple is dedicated to Rudreshwara (Shiva), Vishnu and Surya, making it a Trikuta (three-shrine) temple. It is famous for its exquisitely carved pillars, polished stone sculptures and advanced engineering techniques. The temple represents the mature stage of Kakatiya architecture, combining artistic excellence with structural innovation. It remains one of the most important historical monuments of Telangana. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Temple – Thousand Pillar Temple
• Dynasty – Kakatiyas
• Builder – Rudradeva
• Location – Hanamkonda

91.s: The main profession of Jayapa who wrote Nritta Ratnavali?
91.x:
Jayapa Senani, the celebrated author of Nritta Ratnavali, served as Gajasahini (Commander of the Elephant Corps) under the Kakatiya ruler Ganapatideva. Although he was a military commander, Jayapa possessed exceptional knowledge of dance and music. His Nritta Ratnavali is one of the most authoritative medieval treatises on Indian dance and describes Marga and Desi dance traditions, dance postures, mudras and performance techniques. The famous dance sculptures of the Ramappa Temple closely follow the principles laid down in this work, making it an invaluable source for the study of medieval Indian dance. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Author – Jayapa Senani
• Position – Gajasahini
• Famous Work – Nritta Ratnavali

91.s: The dance sculptures at Ramappa Temple in Palampet were carved according to the principles of which book of dance science?
o: A treatise on dance in the Marga Saili style
A treatise on dance in the Desi style
91.x:
The Ramappa Temple at Palampet, built during the Kakatiya period, is one of the finest examples of medieval temple architecture and sculpture in India. It is especially famous for its beautifully carved Madanikas (bracket figures) depicting various dance postures. These sculptures closely follow the principles laid down in Nrittaratnavali, a celebrated treatise on dance written by Jayapa Senani, the commander-in-chief of the Kakatiya ruler Ganapatideva. Nrittaratnavali is one of the most important medieval works on Indian dance. It describes both Marga (classical) and Desi (regional) dance traditions, dance postures, hand gestures, movements and performance techniques. The Ramappa sculptures are regarded as a visual representation of the dance forms described in this treatise. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Author – Jayapa Senani
• Work – Nrittaratnavali
• Temple – Ramappa Temple, Palampet
• UNESCO World Heritage Site – Ramappa Temple (2021)

93.s: Arrange the following Reddi rulers in chronological order. A. Kumaragiri Reddi B. Anavema Reddi C. Anavota Reddi D. Pedakomati Vema Reddi
93.x:
The Reddi Kingdom was founded by Prolaya Vema Reddi after the decline of the Kakatiyas. The rulers mentioned in this question succeeded one another in the following order: Anavota Reddi succeeded Prolaya Vema Reddi and consolidated the newly established kingdom. He was followed by Anavema Reddi, who further strengthened the administration and expanded the kingdom. After him came Kumaragiri Reddi, who was an able administrator and a great patron of literature, music and dance. His court became an important centre of Telugu culture. Finally, Pedakomati Vema Reddi ascended the throne. He was both a scholar and a capable ruler and continued the literary traditions established by his predecessors. Therefore, the correct chronological order is: Anavota Reddi → Anavema Reddi → Kumaragiri Reddi → Pedakomati Vema Reddi Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Founder – Prolaya Vema Reddi
• Capital – Addanki (later Kondavidu)
• Greatest literary patron – Kumaragiri Reddi

93.x:
Lakuma Devi was the celebrated court dancer of Kumaragiri Reddy. She was renowned for her mastery over dance and music and greatly influenced the cultural life of the Reddy court. Kumaragiri Reddy himself was a great patron of fine arts, and his court became an important centre for literature, music and dance. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

• Patron – Kumaragiri Reddy

Palkuriki Somanatha was one of the greatest Shaivite poets of the Kakatiya period. 32.s: The attempt of Alauddin Khalji to control the market prices
32.x: The attempt by Alauddin Khalji to control the market prices was highly successful. Alauddin Khalji's measures to control the market prices were one of the most important policy initiatives of his reign. Since Alauddin wanted to maintain a vast standing army, he therefore, lowered the prices of the commodities of daily use. He established separate markets in Delhi, (a) Grain Market (Mandi) (b) Clothes and Groceries market for clothes, sugar, dry fruits, butter and oil (c) Market for horses, slaves, cattle etc. (d) Market for miscellaneous commodities. To ensure implementation, each market was under the control of a superintendent called Shahna-i-Mandi who was assisted by an intelligence officer. Apart from Shahnai-Mandi Alauddin received daily reports of the market from two other independent sources, barids (intelligence officer) and munhiyans (Secret spies).

xa: The dynasty **fell soon after his death in 1316**.
Criticism: controls may have been **confined to Delhi**, and they hurt **merchants and peasants**.

32.s: With which dynasty are token currency, transfer of capital and canals associated?
32.x: The Tughlaqs are known for token currency, capital transfer and canals; the Khaljis for market control and the Lodis as the first Afghan dynasty.
xa: Khaljis' contribution also included **taxation reforms**.
Alauddin's reign = the **"imperial period"**.

32.s: Who is the main source for Alauddin Khalji's market control measures?
32.x: Barani is the main source; Mubarak Shah later abolished the controls.
xa: UPPSC keys call the market control **"highly successful"**.
Prices stayed **stable** during Alauddin's reign.

32.s: Which Sultan abolished Alauddin Khalji's price controls and restored confiscated lands after ascending the throne?
32.x: Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah (1316–1320) abolished the price controls, restored confiscated lands and withdrew the harsh regulations.

32.s: In which work is Ziauddin Barani's account of Alauddin Khalji's reforms found?
32.x: Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, the main account of the reforms; Khazain-ul-Futuh is by Amir Khusrau.

32.s: Who wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh, describing Alauddin Khalji's campaigns?
32.x: Amir Khusrau, who went on the 1310 campaign, wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh.

32.s: Which was the first Afghan dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
32.x: The Lodis were the first Afghan dynasty; they founded Agra.

32.s: Which pair of Delhi Sultanate dynasty and key contribution is wrongly matched?
32.x: Agra was founded by the Lodis; the Tughlaqs are known for token currency, capital transfer and canals.

32.s: Which dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate founded Agra?
32.x: The Lodis, the first Afghan dynasty, founded Agra.

32.s: Which of the following is regarded as a major significance of Alauddin Khalji’s economic and revenue measures?
o: They made religious institutions solely responsible for land measurement.
They introduced paper currency and decentralised all revenue administration.
They introduced the first state-run price-control and rationing system in India and the first land measurement for revenue.
They abolished all forms of taxation and ended state supervision of markets.
32.x: Alauddin’s measures are regarded as the first state-run price-control and rationing system in India and the first land measurement system for revenue assessment.
32.tq: Select the option containing both linked historical significances without an exaggerated claim.
xs: They were the **first state-run price control and rationing system** in India and the **first land measurement for revenue** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Land was measured in **biswa**; granaries rationed grain in scarcity.
There was no paper currency and no end of taxation — taxes like **ghari** and **charai** were added.
xa: His reign = **"imperial period"** of the Sultanate.
Despotism and heavy spying hollowed out the state.

32.s: Alauddin Khalji’s reign is often called the ‘imperial period’ of the Delhi Sultanate mainly because it was marked by:
o: the replacement of the Sultanate by the Bahmani kingdom
the exclusive supremacy of the ulema over state policy
extensive conquests, strong centralisation and imperial ambitions
the abandonment of expansion and the growth of provincial independence
32.x: Alauddin’s extensive conquests, centralised administration, strong army and imperial ambitions led his reign to be described as the imperial period of the Sultanate.
32.tq: Infer the historical label from the cluster of policies and achievements.
xs: The reign shows **extensive conquests, strong centralisation and imperial ambitions** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Alauddin dreamed of being **Sikandar-i-Sani** and ran **harsh, centralised** rule.
The **ulema** were overridden, not supreme.
xa: Firsts: **state-run price control**, **rationing**, **land measurement** for revenue.
Kafur's campaigns reached **Madurai** (**1311**).

33.s: Between which years is the Tughlaq period of the Delhi Sultanate generally placed?
33.x: The Tughlaq period began with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320 and ended when Khizr Khan took Delhi in 1414.
33.tq: Identify the dynasty's beginning and end points rather than confusing it with neighbouring dynasties.
xs: The Tughlaq period runs **1320 to 1414** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It began with **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq Shah in 1320** and ended when **Khizr Khan** took Delhi in **1414**.
xa: Ghiyasuddin ruled **1320-25**; Firoz **1351-88**.
**Timur's invasion** came in **1398**.

33.s: What was the earlier name of Muhammad bin Tughlaq?
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq was called Juna Khan (also Ulugh Khan) before he became Sultan; Ghazi Malik was his father Ghiyasuddin.

33.s: Whom did Ghazi Malik kill to become Sultan Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320?
33.x: Ghazi Malik, earlier governor of Punjab, killed Khusrau Shah and became Sultan in 1320.
xa: He built the **Tughlaqabad** fort.
He was the **first Sultan to start irrigation/canal works**.

33.s: To about what share did Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq limit any increase in land revenue?
33.x: Ghiyasuddin limited any increase to about one-tenth and raised it gradually, besides drought remission and cultivation of waste land.
xa: He was the **first Sultan to start canal works**; **Firoz** dug the most.
He improved the **postal system** with runners and horsemen.

33.s: During whose reign was Warangal conquered and renamed Sultanpur?
33.x: Warangal fell in 1323 during Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's reign and was renamed Sultanpur.
33.tq: Link the conquered place, its new name and the ruler responsible for the conquest.
xs: Warangal fell in **1323** under **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** and was renamed **Sultanpur** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The attack was led by Prince **Juna Khan** (later **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**).
xa: Andhra was then run by **Malik Burhanuddin** of Devagiri, assisted by **Malik Maqbul**.
**Prataparudra II** was taken towards Delhi and died in the **Narmada**.

33.s: In which year did Warangal fall to the Tughlaq forces after a five-month siege?
33.x: Juna Khan first attacked Warangal in 1321-22; it fell after a five-month siege in 1323, before Ghiyasuddin's death in 1325.

33.s: Where did Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq die in 1325 when a wooden pavilion collapsed?
33.x: He died at Afghanpur in 1325 (Ibn Battuta suspected Juna Khan); he had built Tughlaqabad.
xa: **Ibn Battuta** suspects a plot by **Juna Khan**.
Cities of Delhi: **Siri** — **Alauddin Khalji**; **Tughlaqabad** — **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**.

33.s: Of which province was Ghazi Malik the Governor against the Mongols under Alauddin Khalji?
33.x: Ghazi Malik (later Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) was Governor of Punjab under Alauddin, guarding against the Mongols.

33.s: Which city of Delhi was built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq?
33.x: Ghiyasuddin built Tughlaqabad; Siri was Alauddin's and Firozabad and Hisar were Firoz's.

33.s: In which river did the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra II die after the fall of Warangal?
33.x: Prataparudra II was taken towards Delhi and died in the Narmada.

33.s: Which Sultan shifted capital from Delhi to Deogiri?

33.s:
Consider the following statements
1.
Assertion (A): Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued a new gold coin which was called Dinar by Ibn Battuta.
2.
Reason (R): Muhammad bin Tughlaq wanted to issue token currency in gold coins to promote trade with West Asian and North African countries.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are individually true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are individually true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a new gold coin known as the Dinar (called Dinar by Ibn Battuta). He also issued a silver coin called the Adli and undertook important currency reforms during his reign. Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a token currency around 1330 CE to tackle the shortage of silver in the royal treasury. Drawing inspiration from the currency system used in China under Kublai Khan, he issued copper coins (Jitals) and set their value at the same level as silver tankas. However, since the concept of token currency was unfamiliar in India and there was no effective control over minting, counterfeit coins were produced on a large scale. The widespread forgery disrupted the economy and undermined public confidence in the currency. Consequently, the Sultan withdrew the scheme and agreed to exchange the copper coins for silver coins.

33.s: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq had transferred his capital from Delhi to –
33.x: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq had shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devgiri). It was one of the most significant experiments of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq. Various factors have been identified for this experiment. According to Barani, Devgiri probably was at the center of his empire. According to Ibn Battuta, the people of Delhi used to write undeferential letters to Sultan. To punish them he decided to make Devgiri his capital. Muhammad Tughluq was also the first Sultan of Delhi who tried to establish the administrative and cultural unity of northern and southern India. Probably this was also the main reason behind making Devgiri his capital. According to Dr. K.A. Nizami, Sultan Qutbuddin Mubarak Khalji had changed the name of Devgiri to Qutbabad and Muhammad Tughluq to Daulatabad.

33.s: For the first time the token currency was introduced in India by :
33.x: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq launched different types of coins during his period and also decided on their reasonable prices. But the circulation of token currency was his specialty. According to Barani, due to lack of silver in treasury and policy of expanding the empire, Muhammad Tughluq had to launch the token currency. The token currency was launched in Iran during the regime of Gaykhatu, though, the experiment was unsuccessful. The token currency was successfully launched during the period of Kublai Khan. Innovative Muhammad- Bin- Tughluq was inspired by them. The modern historian also notes that there was a shortage of silver all over the world, and there was a severe shortage of silver in India too. Due to this reason, he launched token currency.

33.s:
Assertion (A): Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq issued a new gold coin which was called Dinar by Ibn Battuta.
Reason (R) : Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq wanted to issue token currency in gold coins to promote trade with West Asian and North African countries.
o: Both ‘A’ and ‘R’ are individually true and ‘R’ is the
Both ‘A’ and ‘R’ are individually true but ‘R’ is not
33.x: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq issued the new gold coins which were called ‘Dinar’ by Ibn Battuta. He issue the token currency in copper or Bronze coins to promote his military power not for trade with the West Asian and the North African countries in token currency of gold. Thus, Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

33.s:
Consider the following statements-
Assertion (A) : The scheme of the token currency of Muhammad Tughluq proved unsuccessful.
Reason (R) : Muhammad Tughluq did not have the proper control over currency issue.
Choose the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are individually true, and (R) is the
Both (A) and (R) are individually true, but (R) is not
33.x: Barani describes the five main schemes of Muhammad Tughluq:- (1) Tax increase in Doab, (2) Devgiri (Daultabad) as Capital, (3) Issuing token currency, (4) Attack on Khurasan and (5) Qarachil expedition. The main reason behind the failure of token currency was that the state had no control over the minting of coins. The value of the token currency was equivalent to the silver value currency. As a result, many fraud mints were formed. The Lagan began to be paid by forged coins.

33.s: In which year did Muhammad bin Tughlaq transfer his capital to Devagiri?
33.x: The capital was transferred in 1327; token currency followed around 1329–30.
xa: Khurasan: a huge army raised, then **disbanded unpaid / unused**.
Qarachil (**Kumaon** hills): **army destroyed in the hills**.

33.s: What did the token currency introduced by Muhammad bin Tughlaq around 1329-30 consist of?
o: Gold and silver coins issued to overcome a gold shortage
Silver and copper coins issued exclusively for the army
Copper and brass coins intended to function as tokens
Lead and potin coins modelled on Satavahana currency
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency in copper and brass because of a shortage of silver. Widespread forgery led to its recall and redemption at heavy cost.
33.tq: Discriminate the metal composition and the economic purpose of the token currency.
xs: The token currency was of **copper and brass**, meant to function as tokens — so option **(3)** is correct.
Cause: a **silver shortage** and the idea of a token coin.
Result: **mass forgery**; the coins were **recalled and redeemed at heavy cost** to the treasury.
xa: It came c. **1329-30**, after the move to Daulatabad (**1327**).
Exam line: "token currency was **copper and brass**".

33.s: What did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's higher taxation of the Doab, coinciding with a famine, lead to?
33.x: Meant to raise revenue, the Doab tax increase coincided with famine and caused peasant revolts and flight.
xa: During the famine the Sultan moved to the **Swarga-dwari** relief camp on the **Ganga** near **Kannauj**.
**Taqavi** (sondhar) loans for seed and wells came from MBT.

33.s: What was the aim of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Qarachil (Kumaon hills) expedition?
33.x: The Qarachil expedition aimed to secure the hill frontier; the Khurasan expedition aimed at Central Asian conquest.
xa: Khurasan army: **disbanded unpaid / unused**; Qarachil army: **destroyed in the hills**.
Barani called MBT a **"mixture of opposites"**.

33.s: Which one of the following is NOT a town associated with Firoz Shah Tughlaq?
33.x: Firozabad, Fatehabad and Hisar Firoza were associated with Firoz Shah. Daulatabad was the renamed capital under Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
33.tq: Find the odd location by separating Firoz Shah's town-building from Muhammad bin Tughlaq's capital transfer.
xs: **Daulatabad** is not a Firoz town — so option **(1)** is the answer.
Daulatabad was **Devagiri**, renamed by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (**1327**).
Firoz founded **Firozabad** (Firoz Shah Kotla), **Fatehabad**, **Hisar Firoza** and **Jaunpur**.
xa: He laid about **1,200** fruit gardens around Delhi.
He moved **Ashokan pillars** from **Topra** and **Meerut** to Delhi.

33.s: For which of the following is Firoz Shah Tughlaq's wazir Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul noted?
o: Paying compensation to people who had suffered under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Introducing token currency in copper and brass
Leading the Qarachil expedition into the Kumaon hills
33.x: Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul paid compensation to persons who had suffered during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rule.
33.tq: Identify the responsible official by matching the administrative action with the correct office-holder.
xs: **Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul** **paid compensation to people who had suffered under Muhammad bin Tughlaq** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Nagarkot texts were translated by **Azizuddin Khalid Khani**; **token currency** and **Qarachil** were **MBT's**.
xa: Maqbul was the Brahmin **Jagannatha Pandit**, converted to Islam.
He had assisted **Malik Burhanuddin** at **Warangal** before becoming Firoz's chief minister.

33.s: How did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Khurasan expedition end?
o: The army being destroyed in the hills
33.x: The army raised for Khurasan was disbanded unpaid; destruction in the hills was the fate of the Qarachil expedition.

33.s: What was the silver coin issued by Muhammad bin Tughlaq called?
33.x: MBT's silver coin was the Adli; his new gold coin was called Dinar by Ibn Battuta.

33.s: Which of the following pairs of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiment and its result is correctly matched?
o: Khurasan expedition – army destroyed in the hills
Transfer of capital – court stayed at Daulatabad
33.x: Token currency led to mass forgery; the Khurasan army was disbanded unpaid, the Qarachil army was destroyed and the court returned to Delhi.

33.s: During Sultanate period, 'Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi' was related with which of the following?
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced the department of Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi for the development of Agriculture. The purpose of the department was to provide direct aid to farmers so as to bring more land under agriculture.

33.s: Which Sultan of Delhi had established a separate Agriculture Department and had planned the ‘rotation of crops’ ?
Which ruler established 'Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi' department?
Diwan-E-Kohi is associated with–
What was the relief and cultivation camp near Kannauj on the Ganga, set up during the famine in Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign, called?
33.x: Swarga-dwari was a famine-relief camp on the Ganga near Kannauj, established for relief and cultivation.
33.tq: Use the place-name association to distinguish a famine-relief camp from Firoz Shah's institutions and towns.
xs: The relief camp was **Swarga-dwari** (Swargadwari), on the **Ganga near Kannauj** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It gave **relief and cultivation** during the **Doab famine**.
**Dar-ul-Shifa** (free hospital) and **Diwan-i-Khairat** (charity) are **Firoz's**; **Firozabad** is his town.
xa: The **Doab tax rise** coincided with the famine; peasants revolted and fled.
MBT gave **taqavi** loans for **seed + wells**.

33.s: With which of the following was the Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi of Muhammad bin Tughlaq mainly concerned?
33.x: Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi was an agriculture department intended to extend cultivation, especially by bringing waste land under the plough.
33.tq: Identify the administrative department from the function assigned to it.
xs: **Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi** was MBT's **agriculture** department to **bring waste land under cultivation** — so option **(4)** is correct (UKPSC **2025**; UPPSC **2017**).
It also pushed farmers towards **better crops**.
Horse branding (**dagh**) and **market control** were **Alauddin's**; **jizya on Brahmins** was **Firoz's**.
xa: ⚠ **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** = MBT; **Diwan-i-Khairat** and **Diwan-i-Bandagan** = Firoz.
**Taqavi** loans were later **written off by Firoz**.

33.s: For what were taqavi (sondhar) loans mainly given during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign?
33.x: Taqavi or sondhar loans were agricultural advances intended to help cultivators purchase seed and dig wells.
33.tq: Match the specialised administrative term with its precise practical purpose.
xs: **Taqavi** (sondhar) loans were for **seeds and wells** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They were MBT's state loans to cultivators.
xa: **Firoz** later **wrote off** MBT's taqavi loans and all debts owed to the state.
MBT's **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** worked to **extend cultivation**.

33.s: According to Ibn Battuta, at what intervals were the horse couriers (uluq) posted?
33.x: Horse couriers were every four miles; foot couriers (dawa) had three stations to every mile.
xa: ⚠ **Uluq** = horse; **dawa** = foot.
Ghiyasuddin had already improved the post with **runners + horsemen**.

33.s: How did the 'dawa' couriers of the Sultanate postal system described by Ibn Battuta travel?
33.x: Dawa were foot couriers; uluq were horse couriers.

33.s: Which rebel was Muhammad bin Tughlaq pursuing when he died at Thatta in 1351?
33.x: MBT died at Thatta on the way to Sindh, chasing the rebel Taghi after a Gujarat revolt.

33.s: "The king was freed from his people and they from their king". On whose death did Badauni comment thus? Medieval Indian History PMF IAS IH – 38
33.x: The remark "The king was freed from his people and they from their king" is attributed to Abdul Qadir Badauni on the death of Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq.

33.s: On the death of which Muslim ruler, a historian said ‘the king was freed from his people and they from their king’?
33.x: When Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was in Daulatabad, a revolt took place in Gujarat led by Taghi. Sultan dashed to Gujarat to quell the revolt. Taghi was defeated and fled to Sindh. After restoring peace in Gujarat, Sultan moved to Sindh to kill Taghi. Sultan fell sick on the way and died on March 20, 1351 A.D., near Thatta. On his death, Badayuni wrote, 'the king was freed from his people and the people from their king'.

33.s: Ibn Battuta, the Moorish traveller, visited India during the reign of :
33.x: Ibn Battuta (1304-1377 A.D.) was an African traveller of Moroccon origin. He came to India during 1333-1342 A.D. in the period of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq. Muhammad-Bin- Tughluq appointed him as Qazi of Delhi. Later in 1342 AD, he was sent to China as an ambassador of Sultan. Ibn Battuta had mentioned about his journey in his book Kitab-ul- Rihla.

33.s: Ibn Battuta visited India during the reign of :
To which country did Muhammad bin Tughlaq send Ibn Battuta, the Qazi of Delhi, as envoy in 1342?
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq made Ibn Battuta Qazi of Delhi and sent him as envoy to China in 1342.
xa: He was a **Moroccan**, born at **Tangiers**, **1304**; real name **Abu Abdullah Muhammad**.
His **Rihla (Kitab-ul-Rehla)** is in **Arabic**.

33.s: Which of the following observations is associated with Ibn Battuta's account of the Delhi Sultanate?
o: Sati was permitted only to members of the royal family.
Sati was completely prohibited throughout the Sultanate.
Sati was not recorded by any contemporary traveller.
33.x: Ibn Battuta recorded the practice of sati and stated that it required the Sultan's permission.
33.tq: Select the precise recorded condition rather than an absolute statement about the practice.
xs: Ibn Battuta records that **sati required the Sultan's permission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He also recorded the **spy system** and the **postal system**.
xa: He found MBT **eccentric**, **severe in temper**, but **generous**.
He was the **first foreign traveller** to visit **Vijayanagara**, in **Harihara I's** reign (APPSC PYQ).

33.s: Which of the following statements about Ibn Battuta’s Rihla is correct?
o: It was written in Arabic and describes conditions in the Sultanate and the Deccan.
It was written in Persian and deals only with Central Asia.
It was written in Hindavi and describes only Vijayanagara.
It was written in Sanskrit under the patronage of Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
33.x: Rihla, also called Kitab-ul-Rehla, was written in Arabic and describes conditions in the Sultanate and the Deccan.
33.tq: Use the language-and-content combination to reject swapped literary traditions.
xs: Rihla **was written in Arabic and describes the Sultanate and the Deccan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is also called **Kitab-ul-Rehla**.
It was not Persian, Hindavi or Sanskrit.
xa: It records **uluq** and **dawa** couriers, the **spy system** and **sati**.
Its author, **Abu Abdullah Muhammad**, was a Moroccan born in **1304**.

33.s: Who described Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a 'mixture of opposites'?
33.x: Barani described Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a 'mixture of opposites'. Ibn Battuta characterised him as eccentric, severe in temper and generous.
33.tq: Separate the judgements of the court chronicler, foreign traveller and other contemporary figures.
xs: **Barani** called MBT a **"mixture of opposites"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Ibn Battuta** called him **eccentric**, **quick-tempered**, but **generous**.
**Badauni** commented on his **death at Thatta (1351)**.
xa: Barani's **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** is the main account of these reigns.
Verdict: experiments **sound in idea, poor in execution**.

33.s: In whose reign did Ibn Battuta, the first foreign traveller to Vijayanagara, visit the kingdom?
33.x: Ibn Battuta is identified in this context as the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara during the reign of Harihara I.
33.tq: Distinguish the earliest associated ruler from the more famous later Vijayanagara monarchs.
xs: Ibn Battuta was the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara, in **Harihara I's** reign (APPSC PYQ) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Vijayanagara was founded in **1336** by **Harihara and Bukka**.
xa: He came to India in **1333** and served MBT as **Qazi of Delhi**.
He was sent as **envoy to China** in **1342**.

33.s: Where was Ibn Battuta born?
33.x: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta (1304-1377) was born at Tangiers.

33.s: Which of the following works was written by Barani?
33.x: Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Fatawa-i-Jahandari; Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi is Firoz's autobiography.

33.s: Which historian remarked on the death of Muhammad bin Tughlaq that 'the king was freed from his people and they from their king'?
33.x: The remark is by Badauni; Barani called MBT a 'mixture of opposites'.

33.s: In which year did Ibn Battuta arrive in India?
33.x: Ibn Battuta came to India in 1333, during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign, and stayed till 1342.

33.s: Which post did Muhammad bin Tughlaq give to Ibn Battuta?
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq made Ibn Battuta the Qazi (judge) of Delhi.

33.s: Who is the author of Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi?
33.x: Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Fatawa-i-Jahandari.

33.s: Who founded the Bahmani Empire?
33.x: In 1347 Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu) revolted against Muhammad bin Tughlaq and founded the Bahmani Empire.

33.s: Which one of the following statements about Malik Maqbul is correct?
o: He established the Bahmani kingdom under the title Hasan Gangu.
He was the founder of the Madurai Sultanate and was known as Ahsan Shah.
He founded Vijayanagara jointly with Harihara and Bukka.
He was originally a captured Brahmin named Jagannatha Pandit and later became Firoz Shah's wazir.
33.x: Malik Maqbul was originally the captured Brahmin Jagannatha Pandit, who converted to Islam and later became Firoz Shah's wazir, Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul.
33.tq: Trace a historical personality through a name change, conversion and later office.
xs: Malik Maqbul **was the captured Brahmin Jagannatha Pandit who became Firoz Shah's wazir** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He converted to Islam and became **Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul**.
**Hasan Gangu** founded the **Bahmani** kingdom; **Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah** the **Madurai Sultanate**; **Harihara and Bukka** Vijayanagara.
xa: After **1323** he assisted **Malik Burhanuddin** of Devagiri at **Warangal**.
As wazir he **paid compensation** to those who had suffered under MBT.

33.s: In which year was the Madurai Sultanate established?
33.x: The Madurai Sultanate dates to 1335, Vijayanagara to 1336 and the Bahmani kingdom to 1347.
xa: Madurai Sultanate: **Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah**.
Bahmani founder: **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah** (**Hasan Gangu**).

33.s: Around which year did the Reddis expel the Tughlaq forces from coastal Andhra?
33.x: Coastal Andhra was freed around 1325, before the Madurai Sultanate (1335), Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmani kingdom (1347).
xa: **Kapaya Nayaka** recaptured Warangal also in **1336**.
These break-aways followed MBT's **badly carried out** schemes.

33.s: Under whose guidance did Harihara and Bukka found Vijayanagara?
33.x: Harihara and Bukka, sent by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, founded Vijayanagara under Vidyaranya's guidance.
xa: **Ibn Battuta** visited Vijayanagara in **Harihara I's** reign.
⚠ In **1336** Kapaya Nayaka also recaptured **Warangal**.

33.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Coastal Andhra liberation — Prolaya Vema Reddi

33.s: Public Works Department was primarily established by-
33.x: The Public Works Department was primarily established by Firuz Shah Tughluq during the Sultanate period. It is said that he established 200 new cities. Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad etc. are some of the main cities established by him. According to Firishta, Firuz had also constructed 40 Mosques, 30 schools, 20 palaces, 100 Inns, 100 hospitals, five tombs, 100 public bathrooms, ten pillars and 150 bridges. He had converted the name Ikdala to Azadpur and Pandua to Firuzabad during his Bengal campaign. Malik Ghazi Shehana was the main architect in his empire. The policy of each building as per its expected expenditure was put in front of ‘Diwan-i-Wazarat,’ only then could the fund be allowed on it.

33.s: The Sultan of Delhi who was very concerned about charity and alms and established a department called ‘Diwan-i-Khairat’ for it, was:

33.s: Which one of the following Sultans of Delhi introduced measures for improving the quality of fruits?

33.s: What was ‘Dar-ul-Shafa’ established by Firuz Tughluq?
Who among the following Sultans of Delhi established an ‘Employment Exchange’ to help the unemployed?
The Sultan of Delhi who is reputed to have built the biggest network of canals in India was
33.x: Feroz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388) is known for constructing the largest canal network among the Delhi Sultans. The longest canal was about 200 kilometres long and ran from the river Sutlej to Hansi. Another canal was between the Yamuna and Hissar. These and other canals were meant for irrigation and water to the new towns he developed.

33.s: The Sultan of Delhi who is reputed to have built the biggest network of canals in India was :
33.x: The reign of Firuz Tughluq is famous for building the biggest network of canals for irrigation purpose. They were:- (1) Sutlej river to Ghaggar (96 miles) (2) Yamuna river to Hisar (150 miles), (3) Hill of Sirmor to Hansi, (4) Ghaggar river to Firozabad and (5) Yamuna river to Firozabad. He also engraved 150 wells for irrigation and betterment of passengers. According to Firista, Firuz built 50 dams and 30 lakes at different places. Firuz Shah was the first Sultan of Delhi who imposed ‘Haqq-i-Sharb’ tax on irrigation. Those farmers who used to irrigate their fields from the water of the royal canal had to give 1/10th part of the produce to the government.

33.s: Who was the last ruler of the Tughluq dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
