48.x: The “Chishtia SufiOrder” was established in Chishti Sharif of Afghanistan by Abu Ishaq Shami Chishti and his disciple Khwaja Abu Ahmad Abdal, but it was primarily established in India by Muinuddin Chishti. He came to India with the army of Muhammad Ghori in 1192 A.D. (12th century) and made Ajmer, Rajasthan his abode. He died in 1236 AD. Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was his disciple.

48.s: The Sufisaint who maintained that devotional music was one way of coming close to God was :
48.x: Muinuddin Chishti introduced the Chishti order of Sufism in India. He maintained that devotional music was one way to come closer to God.

48.s: The spread of which of the following Sufisect was mostly limited to Sindh, Multan and Punjab?
48.x: The Suhrawardi SufiSect entered India at about the same time as Chishtis sect but its activities were confined largely to the Punjab, Multan and Sindh. This SufiSect was established in India by Baha-Ud-Din Zakariya.

48.s: Who among the following does not belong to the Chishti order?
48.x: Chishti order is a Sunni Sufiorder within the mystic Sufitradition of Islam. Muinuddin Chishti introduced the Chishti order in India. Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was a saint of Chishti order from Delhi; Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya was a saint of Chishti order in Indian sub-continent. Shaikh Abdul Jilani did not belong to Chishti Silsila. Rather, he founded Qadiri order.

48.s: The most orthodox Sufiorder was –
48.x: Baha-ud-Din Naqshband founded the SufiNaqshbandi order in 14th century. This order was made popular in India by Babur. Insistence on rigid adherence to Shariat and nurturing love for Prophet was the essence of this order. According to Jharkhand Public Service Commission, option (b) is the correct answer.

48.s: Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria belonged to which sect?
48.x: Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria started Suhrawardi order in India. Shaikh Sadr-ud-din Arif, Shaikh Rakh-ud-din Abul Fateh and Shaikh Jalaluddin Surkh were associated with this Sufisect.

48.s: Which Sufi order was strictly orthodox and opposed Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul?
48.x: The Naqshbandis opposed Sulh-i-Kul; the Chishtis kept aloof from the court, the Suhrawardis accepted royal service and the Shattaris absorbed yogic practices.
xa: ⚠ Chishti (aloof, sama) vs Suhrawardi (close to court) = **most-asked contrast**; Naqshbandi = the **orthodox pole**.
Naqshbandis also opposed **Shia influence**.

48.s: With whom did the Naqshbandi order originate in Central Asia?
48.x: The order began with Bahauddin Naqshband; in India it was associated with Khwaja Baqi Billah and Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi.
xa: Naqshbandis were the **most orthodox** (JPSC 2016); **opposed sama** and visits to saints' tombs.
Sirhindi was **imprisoned by Jahangir**.

48.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior — Shattari order
48.x: Abdul Qadir Jilani founded the Qadiri order; he was not a Chishti saint. Shah Abdullah Shattari, Muhammad Ghaus and Sharafuddin Yahya Maneri are correctly associated with the orders shown.
48.tq: The wrong-founder trap distinguishes Abdul Qadir Jilani from the Chishti order.
xs: **Abdul Qadir Jilani — Chishti** is wrong — option **(1)** is the answer; he **founded the Qadiri order** (RPSC 2016).
**Shah Abdullah Shattari** founded the **Shattari** order; **Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior** was Shattari.
**Sharafuddin Yahya Maneri** belongs to the **Firdausi** order of **Bihar**.
xa: Chishti founder at Chisht (Herat): **Khwaja Abu Ishaq Shami**; in India **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti**.
**Mahdawi** order = **Syed Muhammad of Jaunpur**.

48.s: Regarding the Naqshbandi order, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Bahauddin Zakariya established its main khanqah at Multan.
Bahauddin Naqshband himself established the order in India during Akbar's reign.
Moinuddin Chishti brought the order to India with Muhammad Ghori.
Khwaja Baqi Billah brought the order to India in the late sixteenth century.
48.x: Bahauddin Naqshband was the Central Asian founder and was revered by Babur, but he did not come to India. Khwaja Baqi Billah brought the Naqshbandi order to India in the late sixteenth century.
48.tq: Separate the original founder outside India from the person who introduced the order in India.
xs: **Khwaja Baqi Billah** brought the Naqshbandi order to India in the **late 16th c.** — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ **Bahauddin Naqshband** founded it in Central Asia but **never came to India**.
**Bahauddin Zakariya** (Multan) was **Suhrawardi**; **Moinuddin Chishti** came with **Muhammad Ghori** as the **Chishti** founder.
xa: The order was revered by **Babur**.
Indian Naqshbandis: **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi**, **Shah Waliullah**, **Shah Abdul Aziz**.

48.s: Which comparison between the Chishti and Suhrawardi orders is correct?
o: Chishtis were close to the court, whereas Suhrawardis rejected sama entirely.
Chishtis were the orthodox pole, whereas Suhrawardis were wandering Qalandars.
Chishtis were generally aloof and associated with sama, whereas Suhrawardis maintained closeness to the court.
Both orders were Be-shara and rejected Islamic law.
48.x: The Chishtis are contrasted with the Suhrawardis as relatively aloof and associated with sama, while the Suhrawardis were closer to the court.
48.tq: Use the central contrast rather than a shared feature.
xs: **Chishtis** were **aloof and associated with sama**; **Suhrawardis** stayed **close to the court** — option **(3)** is correct.
The **orthodox pole** was the **Naqshbandi**, not the Chishti; **Qalandars** were Be-shara wanderers.
Both Chishti and Suhrawardi were **Ba-shara**, following Sharia.
xa: ⚠ This Chishti vs Suhrawardi contrast is the **most-asked** one.
Bahauddin Zakariya (Suhrawardi) got the title **Shaikh-ul-Islam** from Iltutmish.

48.s: Where did the Firdausi order, led by Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri, flourish?
48.x: The Firdausis followed Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri in Bihar; the Suhrawardis followed Bahauddin Zakariya in Multan and Sindh.
n: The Suhrawardi Sufi Silsilah is associated with Bahauddin Zakariya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Suhrawardi Sufi Silsilah is associated with Multan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Suhrawardi Sufi Silsilah is associated with Punjab. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Suhrawardi Sufi Silsilah is associated with Sindh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Firdausia Sufi Silsilah is associated with Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Firdausia Sufi Silsilah is associated with Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Naqshbandi Sufi Silsilah opposed Sama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Naqshbandi Sufi Silsilah emphasized Shariat. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Ahmad Sirhindi was associated with the Naqshbandi Sufi Silsilah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Qadiri Sufi Silsilah followed the tradition of Abdul Qadir Jilani. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: **Chishti** — **Muinuddin Chishti**, **Ajmer**.
Bahauddin Zakariya backed **Iltutmish against Qabacha** and got the title **Shaikh-ul-Islam**.
⚠ **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** = Qadiri/Chishti; **Wahdat-ush-Shuhud** = Sirhindi (Naqshbandi).

48.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of saints belonging to the Chishti Silsila?
o: Miyan Mir, Muhibullah Shah, Dara Shikoh and Burhanuddin Gharib
Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi, Burhanuddin Gharib, Gesudaraz and Hamiduddin of Nagaur
Khwaja Baqi Billah, Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, Shah Waliullah and Hamiduddin Nagori
Bahauddin Zakariya, Ruknuddin Abul Fath, Jalaluddin Tabrizi and Gesudaraz
48.x: Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi, Burhanuddin Gharib, Gesudaraz and the Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur are all associated with the Chishti order.
48.tq: Use group identification to separate closely related saints belonging to different Sufi orders.
xs: **Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi, Burhanuddin Gharib, Gesudaraz and Hamiduddin of Nagaur** are all Chishtis — option **(2)** is correct.
**Miyan Mir, Muhibullah Shah, Dara Shikoh** = **Qadiri**; **Baqi Billah, Sirhindi, Shah Waliullah** = **Naqshbandi**.
**Bahauddin Zakariya, Ruknuddin Abul Fath, Jalaluddin Tabrizi** = **Suhrawardi**.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC 2018:** **Gesudaraz** = the Chishti in the list.
Other Chishtis: **Moinuddin**, **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki**, **Baba Farid**, **Nizamuddin Auliya**.

48.s: Qazi Hamiduddin Nagori belonged to which Sufi order?
48.x: Qazi Hamiduddin Nagori was a Suhrawardi, unlike the Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur, a disciple of Moinuddin Chishti.
xa: ⚠ Some notes list "Hamiduddin Nagori" under the Suhrawardis — keep the two apart.
Moinuddin Chishti (**1143-1235**) has his dargah at **Ajmer**.

48.s: Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last Qutb Shahi ruler of Golconda, was a disciple of which saint?
48.x: Abul Hasan Tana Shah was a disciple of the Chishti saint Shah Raju Qattal.
48.tq: Use the ruler–saint association to avoid confusing different Sufi personalities.
xs: **Abul Hasan Tana Shah**, last Qutb Shahi, was a disciple of the Chishti saint **Shah Raju Qattal** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Sirhindi** was Naqshbandi; **Bahauddin Zakariya** was Suhrawardi of Multan; **Bakhtiyar Kaki** was a Delhi Chishti.
xa: At **Golconda**, Sufi gurus settled and Sufism **"gained immense popularity"**.
Golconda khanqahs = **higher-education centres**.

48.s: Dara Shikoh and Miyan Mir belonged to which Sufi order?
48.x: Miyan Mir, Muhibullah Shah and Dara Shikoh were Qadiris.

48.s: Shah Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior belonged to which order?
48.x: Shah Muhammad Ghaus was a Shattari saint, close to Humayun and Tansen; he wrote Jawahir-e-Khamsa.

48.s: Where is Chisht, from which the Chishti order takes its name?
48.x: Chisht is a town in Afghanistan, not a village in Ajmer.

48.s: In which year did Moinuddin Chishti come to India with the army of Muhammad Ghori?
48.x: Moinuddin Chishti came with Muhammad Ghori's army in 1192 and settled at Ajmer.

48.s: Who brought the Naqshbandi order to India in the late 16th century?
48.x: Baqi Billah brought the order to India; Bahauddin Naqshband never came to India.

48.s: Abdul Qadir Jilani founded which Sufi order?
48.x: Abdul Qadir Jilani of Baghdad founded the Qadiri order; he was not a Chishti.

48.s: Who founded the Suhrawardi order of Sufis?
48.x: The Suhrawardi order was founded by Shihabuddin Suhrawardi at Baghdad; Bahauddin Zakariya established it in India.

48.s: Who wrote Jawahir-e-Khamsa?
48.x: Shah Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior, a Shattari Sufi close to Humayun and Tansen, wrote Jawahir-e-Khamsa.

48.s: Which of the following order of Sufism was against music :
48.x: Naqshbandi order was founded by Bahauddin Naqshband during the 14th century. Khwaja Khawand was the important saint of this order who came to India and made Kashmir as the centre of his activities. The promotion of this sect was mainly started around the (1563-1603) A.D., who came to Kabul on orders of his master. Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi also known as Mujaddid (the reformer of Islam) was his disciple. He propounded Wahdat-ul-Shuhud (positivist philosophy) which was against the order Sama (Music). It was the most radical order among Sufis. He also opposed liberal policies of Akbar. Aurangzeb was also influenced by this Sufiorder.

48.s: What did the early Chishtis avoid that the later Deccan Chishtis accepted?
48.x: Early Chishtis avoided court patronage and state grants, while later Deccan Chishtis accepted grants; they encouraged sama and qawwali.
xa: The **Naqshbandis** opposed sama.
**Amir Khusrau**, disciple of Nizamuddin, introduced **Qaul**.

48.s: Bahauddin Zakariya was given which title after supporting Iltutmish against Qabacha?
48.x: Bahauddin Zakariya received the title Shaikh-ul-Islam after backing Iltutmish against Qabacha.
48.tq: Test the exact title associated with a named Sufi saint.
xs: **Bahauddin Zakariya** backed **Iltutmish against Qabacha** and got the title **Shaikh-ul-Islam** — option **(3)** is correct.
He was the **Suhrawardi** saint of **Multan**; the order stayed close to rulers.
xa: ⚠ Chishti = aloof + sama; Suhrawardi = court + **Shaikh-ul-Islam**; Naqshbandi = most orthodox.
Suhrawardis accepted **wealth and posts**.

48.s: Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-Kul and was subsequently imprisoned by which Mughal ruler?
48.x: Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-Kul and was imprisoned during the reign of Jahangir.
48.tq: Separate the ruler whose policy was criticised from the ruler who ordered the imprisonment.
xs: **Ahmad Sirhindi** criticised Akbar's **Sulh-i-Kul** and was **imprisoned by Jahangir** — option **(2)** is correct.
As a strictly orthodox **Naqshbandi**, he opposed Sulh-i-Kul and **Shia influence**.
xa: Sirhindi's title: **Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani**.
He propounded **Wahdat-ush-Shuhud** against Wahdat-ul-Wujud.
His works: **Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani** (letters), **Radd-i-Khawafiq** (anti-Shia tract).

48.s: Ahmad Sirhindi was known by which title?
48.x: Ahmad Sirhindi of the Naqshbandi order was called Mujaddid Alif Sani, the reviver of the second Islamic millennium. Chirag-i-Delhi was Nasiruddin Mahmud and Mehboob-i-Ilahi was Nizamuddin Auliya.
48.tq: Link each title to its saint.
n: Nizamuddin Auliya was known as Mehboob-i-Ilahi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Nasiruddin Mahmud was known as Chirag-i-Delhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Salim Chishti was known as Shaikh-ul-Hind. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Ahmad Sirhindi was known as Mujaddid Alif Sani. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Ahmad Sirhindi is associated with Wahdat-ul-Shuhud. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
xs: Ahmad Sirhindi was called **Mujaddid Alif Sani** — option **(4)**.
He belonged to the **Naqshbandi** order.
**Chirag-i-Delhi** = **Nasiruddin Mahmud**; **Mehboob-i-Ilahi** = **Nizamuddin Auliya**; **Shaikh-ul-Hind** = **Salim Chishti**.
xa: Sirhindi criticised Akbar's **Sulh-i-Kul** and was **imprisoned by Jahangir**.
He propounded **Wahdat-ush-Shuhud** ("Unity of Appearance").
His letters: **Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani**; anti-Shia tract: **Radd-i-Khawafiq**.

48.s: Nizamuddin Auliya saw the reign of seven or more Sultans of Delhi but:
48.x: Nizamuddin Auliya stayed aloof from the state and never visited the Sultans' court.

48.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Naqshbandi order?
o: It was the most orthodox order
48.x: The Naqshbandis were the most orthodox order; they opposed sama and tomb visits and condemned bid'at.

48.s:
Consider the following statements about the Suhrawardi order:
1. It kept aloof from rulers and refused state service.
2. Bahauddin Zakariya backed Iltutmish against Qabacha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
48.x: Bahauddin Zakariya backed Iltutmish against Qabacha and became Shaikh-ul-Islam; the Suhrawardis stayed close to rulers, so statement 1 is wrong.

48.s: The Mausoleum (Dargah) of which Chishti Saint was visited by Akbar ?
48.x: Akbar supported Chishti sect expressing his faith in Sufism. He sought the company of the religious divine saints with whom he conversed with inborn zeal and humility. He frequently visited the Mausoleum of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and the shrine of contemporary Sufisage Shaikh Salim Chishti at Sikri.

48.s: Who was popularly known as Chiragh-i-Delhi ?
48.x: Shaikh Nasiruddin Mahmud was a disciple of Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya. He was given the title of 'Chirag-i-Dehlavi'.

48.s: Who among the following was given the title of Shaikh-ul-Hind’?
48.x: The name of Shaikh Salim Chishti is noteworthy among the saints of Chishti Sufiorder. He was the son of Shaikh Bahauddin. He lived in Arabia for a long period and was awarded by the title of ‘Shaikh-ul-Hind.’ After returning from Arabia, he started living in Sikri situated about 37 km away from Agra which was later developed as Fatehpur Sikri by Akbar. It is believed that Jahangir was born with the blessings of Shaikh Salim Chishti.

48.s: Who was the guru of Nizamuddin Auliya?
48.x: Nizamuddin Auliya, born at Badaun and buried in Delhi, was a disciple of Baba Farid.
xa: Dates **1238-1325**; title **Mahboob-i-Ilahi**.
His hospice drew both **common people and nobles**.
**Amir Khusrau**, his disciple, introduced **Qaul** in Qawwali.

48.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Banda Nawaz or Gesudaraz — Muhammad Hussaini Gesudaraz
48.x: ‘Garib Nawaz’ is associated with Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, not Nasiruddin Mahmud.
xs: **Garib Nawaz — Nasiruddin Mahmud** is wrong — option **(3)** is the answer; Garib Nawaz is **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti**.
**Nasiruddin Mahmud** is **Chiragh-i-Delhi**, the last great Chishti saint of Delhi.
**Banda Nawaz = Gesudaraz**, **Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani = Sirhindi**, **Ganj-i-Shakar = Baba Farid** are correct.
xa: **Mahboob-i-Ilahi** = **Nizamuddin Auliya** (UKPSC 2016).
**Data Ganj Bakhsh** = **Ali Hujwiri**.
Moinuddin Chishti (**1143-1235**) has his dargah at **Ajmer**.

48.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi — Data Ganj Bakhsh
48.x: Baba Farid, also known as Fariduddin Masud, was called Ganj-i-Shakar. Data Ganj Bakhsh was the title of Ali Hujwiri, while Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani was the title of Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi.
48.tq: Use the exact title–person association and eliminate swapped titles.
xs: **Baba Farid — Ganj-i-Shakar** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Chiragh-i-Delhi** = **Nasiruddin Mahmud**; **Data Ganj Bakhsh** = **Ali Hujwiri**.
**Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani** = **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi**, not Banda Nawaz.
xa: **Banda Nawaz** = **Muhammad Hussaini Gesudaraz** of **Gulbarga**.
**Garib Nawaz** = **Moinuddin Chishti**; **Mahboob-i-Ilahi** = **Nizamuddin Auliya**.

48.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Naqshbandi order – Disciple of Muinuddin Chishti
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki – Teacher of Nizamuddin Auliya
48.x: Nizamuddin Auliya was called Mehboob-i-Ilahi and Sultan-ul-Mashaikh; Bakhtiyar Kaki was Muinuddin Chishti's disciple, Baba Farid taught Nizamuddin, and the Naqshbandis opposed sama.
n: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was a Chishti saint. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was a disciple of Muinuddin Chishti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Baba Farid was associated with the Chishti order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Baba Farid was the teacher of Nizamuddin Auliya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Nizamuddin Auliya was associated with the Chishti order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Nizamuddin Auliya was called Mehboob-i-Ilahi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Nizamuddin Auliya was called Sultan-ul-Mashaikh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Naqshbandi Sufi Silsilah opposed Sama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: Baba Farid's compositions are in the **Guru Granth Sahib**.
**Amir Khusrau**, Nizamuddin's disciple, introduced **Qaul**, the opening hymn of Qawwali.
Nizamuddin Auliya (**1238-1325**) was born at **Badaun**.

48.s: Amir Khusrau, the disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, introduced which element of Qawwali?
o: Fana, the final stage of spiritual union
48.x: Amir Khusrau introduced Qaul, the opening hymn of Qawwali.
48.tq: Associate a cultural contribution with its contributor.
xs: **Amir Khusrau** introduced **Qaul**, the opening hymn of Qawwali — option **(1)** is correct.
**Malfuzat** are recorded conversations; **Fana** is annihilation of self in God; **Khanqah** is a hospice — none is a Qawwali element.
xa: Khusrau was a disciple of **Nizamuddin Auliya**.
The **Chishtis encouraged sama and qawwali**; the Naqshbandis opposed sama.

48.s: Who wrote Kashf-ul-Mahjub?
48.x: Ali Hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh), considered the first prominent Sufi in India, wrote Kashf-ul-Mahjub.
xa: **Siyar-ul-Auliya** = **Mir Khwurd Kirmani** (tazkira); **Akhbar-ul-Akhyar** = **Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi**.
⚠ FIRST = **Ali Hujwiri**; last great Chishti of Delhi = **Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi**.

48.s: Where is the dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki?
48.x: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, disciple of Moinuddin, is buried at Mehrauli in Delhi.

48.s: Where is the dargah of Salim Chishti?
48.x: Salim Chishti (Shaikh-ul-Hind) is buried at Fatehpur Sikri.

48.s: Which Sufi saint is known as Garib Nawaz?
48.x: Garib Nawaz is Moinuddin Chishti; Mahboob-i-Ilahi is Nizamuddin and Ganj-i-Shakar is Baba Farid.

48.s: Besides Nizamuddin Auliya, which disciple of Baba Farid is known as 'Kaliyari'?
48.x: Baba Farid's disciples were Nizamuddin Auliya and Alauddin Sabir (Kaliyari).

48.s: Hamiduddin of Nagaur, a disciple of Moinuddin Chishti, belonged to which order?
48.x: Hamiduddin of Nagaur was a Chishti; Qazi Hamiduddin Nagori was a Suhrawardi.

48.s:
Consider the following statements about Chishti saints:
1. Baba Farid was called Ganj-i-Shakar.
2. Moinuddin Chishti's dargah is at Ajmer.
3. Nizamuddin Auliya lived at Multan.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
48.x: Baba Farid was Ganj-i-Shakar and Moinuddin's dargah is at Ajmer; Nizamuddin lived at Ajodhan and Delhi, not Multan.

48.s: By what name is Baba Farid also known?
48.x: Baba Farid was called Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar; his verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
n: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki belonged to the Chishti order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was a disciple of Muinuddin Chishti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Baba Farid is also known as Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
Baba Farid's compositions are included in the Guru Granth Sahib. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 132-134]
xa: Kaki's dargah is at **Delhi** (Mehrauli); the Qutub Minar's first storey was dedicated to him by **Aibak**.
Baba Farid's dargah is at **Ajodhan** (Pakpattan).
Baba Farid was the **teacher** of **Nizamuddin Auliya**.

48.s: Who is considered the first prominent Sufi in India?
48.x: Ali Hujwiri is considered the first prominent Sufi in India. Moinuddin Chishti later founded the Chishti order in India at Ajmer.
48.tq: Distinguish the first prominent Sufi from the founder of a particular Sufi order in India.
xs: **Ali Hujwiri** (Data Ganj Bakhsh) was the **first prominent Sufi in India** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Moinuddin Chishti** came later as the Chishti founder in India, settling at **Ajmer**.
**Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi** was the **last great Chishti of Delhi**; **Nizamuddin Auliya** was Baba Farid's disciple.
xa: Ali Hujwiri wrote **Kashf-ul-Mahjub**; its themes are love and knowledge of God and **fana**.
⚠ FIRST = **Ali Hujwiri**; LAST great Chishti of Delhi = **Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi**.

48.s: What is ‘Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani’?
o: An anti-Shia tract by Abdul Haqq Dehlavi
A tazkira written by Mir Khwurd Kirmani

49.s: Which one of the following was the difference between Bhakti devotion and formal Sufi religious practice?
o: Bhakti rejected personal devotion, whereas Sufism confined worship to idol rituals.
Bhakti emphasised Vedic ritual, whereas Sufism rejected all forms of devotion.
Bhakti stressed devotion over Vedic ritual, while Sufism valued inner experience over formal Shariat.
Both movements exclusively supported priestly authority and formal ritual.
49.x: Bhakti traditions placed devotion above Vedic ritual and priestly mediation, while Sufism emphasised inner spiritual experience rather than merely formal observance of the Shariat.

xs: **Bhakti** put devotion over **Vedic ritual and priests**; **Sufism** put **inner experience over the formal Shariat** — option **(3)** is correct.
Neither movement backed priestly authority or idol rituals, so options (1), (2), (4) are wrong.
xa: The **guru / pir** bond was central to both.

49.x: Both valued the guide-disciple bond, devotion over ritual and vernacular preaching; exclusive idol worship was not common to them.

49.s: Whose rigid orthodoxy did Kabir and Nanak criticise?

49.s: Which one of the following developments represents the later limitation of the Bhakti and Sufi movements?

xa: Other limitation: **Naqshbandi orthodoxy** pushed back against Sufi-Bhakti liberalism.
Criticism: **egalitarian preaching did not dismantle caste**.

49.s: Which Sufi equated 'Alakh Niranjan' with 'Khuda' in Hindi verse?

xs: **Hamiduddin Nagori** equated **'Alakh Niranjan'** with **'Khuda'** in Hindi verse — option **(2)** is correct.

**Sheikh Nuruddin** founded the **Rishi movement** (Kashmir).

xs: Nathpanthi Hath Yoga belongs to the **Kanphata** yogis of **Gorakhnath's** Nath tradition — option **(4) Gorakhnath**.

49.s: Which one of the following statements about Nizamuddin Auliya and yogic ideas is correct?

**Amritakund** was translated in the **13th century**, but the notes do not credit Nizamuddin with it.

**Hamiduddin Nagori** equated **'Alakh Niranjan'** with **'Khuda'**.

49.x: Hath Yoga was practised by the Nathpanthi yogis of Gorakhnath's tradition, and Sufis adopted techniques such as breath control.

It spread in Andhra through **Mallikarjuna, Inpati and Manchana Panditas**.

49.s: With whom are the early feelings of national awakening among the Marathas through the Bhakti movement linked?
o: Kabir, Dadu Dayal and Guru Nanak
49.x: Among the Marathas, early national awakening was associated with Tukaram, Ramdas and Shivaji.
49.tq: Use the regional grouping of personalities rather than choosing a general Bhakti figure.
xs: Maratha national awakening is linked with **Tukaram, Ramdas and Shivaji** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Tukaram and Ramdas** shaped the Maratha movement under **Shivaji**.
xa: The other echo was among the **Sikhs** (early Sikh awakening).
Bhakti also **revived Hinduism around devotion** and weakened **priestly dominance**.

49.s: What did the interaction between Bhakti and Sufi traditions lead to?
49.x: Bhakti-Sufi interaction produced a composite Indo-Islamic culture, with shrines and vernacular traditions acting as shared spaces.
49.tq: Identify the broad cultural result of the interaction.
xs: Bhakti-Sufi interaction produced a **composite Indo-Islamic culture** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Shared Sufi shrines** and **vernacular** traditions were its common spaces, not Sanskritic or purely Persian culture.
xa: Political echo: **early Sikh and Maratha awakening**.
Limitation: sects **hardened into separate panths**.

49.s: With which region is the Rishi movement associated?
49.x: The Rishi movement belongs to Kashmir; Dadupanth to Rajasthan and Mahanubhava to Maharashtra.
xa: Founders: **Dadu Dayal** (Dadupanth), **Chakradhara** (Mahanubhava), **Sheikh Nuruddin** (Rishi movement).
**Sikhism**: **Guru Nanak** (b. **1469**, Talwandi), Punjab.
**Lingayat / Veerasaiva**: **Basaveswara**, Karnataka and Andhra.

49.s: Which of the following pairs (followers – tradition) is correctly matched?
49.x: Basava's followers are the Lingayats; Lakulisha founded Pashupata Shaivism, Matsyendranath the Nathpanth, and Guru Nanak's followers are Sikhs.
n: Lakulisha's followers followed Pashupata Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Basav's followers followed the Lingayat tradition. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Basav's followers followed the Shaiva tradition. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Matsyendranath's followers followed Nathpanth. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Guru Nanak's followers followed Sikhism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
xa: Guru Nanak was born in **1469** at **Talwandi**.
**Lingayat / Veerasaiva**: founded by **Basaveswara**; spread in **Karnataka** and **Andhra**.
⚠ **Gorakhnath**'s **Kanphata** yogis practised **Hath Yoga**, which Sufis adopted.

49.s: Who founded the Mahanubhava sect of Maharashtra?
49.x: The Mahanubhava sect was founded by Chakradhar Swami in Maharashtra.

49.s: The Dadupanth arose in which region?
49.x: Dadupanth was founded by Dadu in Rajasthan.

49.s: In which year was Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi promulgated?
49.x: Akbar launched Din-i-Ilahi in 1582.

49.s: Dara Shikoh, who continued Akbar's syncretic line, belonged to which Sufi order?
49.x: Dara Shikoh was a Qadiri; Sirhindi, a Naqshbandi, attacked the syncretic line.

49.s: Of which faith was Kharavela a follower?
49.x: Kharavela was a Jain, not an Ajivika; the Ajivikas go back to Makkhali Gosala.

49.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Gupta rulers – Tamil devotees of Vishnu
49.x: Heliodorus set up the Garuda pillar at Besnagar as a Bhagavata; the Alvars worshipped Vishnu, the Nayanars Shiva, and the Gupta kings took the title Parama-bhagavata.
n: Alvar Saints followed Vaishnavism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Alvar Saints were devoted to Vishnu. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Nayanar Saints followed Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Nayanar Saints were devoted to Shiva. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Heliodorus followed the Bhagavata Religion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Gupta rulers followed Vaishnavism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
xa: The **Chalukya rulers** of **Eastern Vengi** also followed **Vaishnavism**.
**Ramanuja**'s followers are known as **Vaishnavas**.
**Lakulisha**'s followers = **Pashupata Shaivism**.

49.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Amoghavarsha I was a disciple of the Jain Acharya Jinasena.
Heliodorus was associated with Bhagavata Religion.
Kharavela of Kalinga was a follower of the Ajivika sect.
49.x: Option C is incorrect: Kharavela of Kalinga was a Jain, as his Hathigumpha inscription shows; the Ajivika sect was founded by Makkhali Gosala. Amoghavarsha I, Heliodorus and the Guptas are correctly described.
49.tq: Recall the religion of each ruler.
n: Heliodorus followed the Bhagavata Religion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Gupta rulers followed Vaishnavism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
Chalukya rulers of Eastern Vengi followed Vaishnavism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 126-127]
xs: The incorrect statement: **Kharavela** followed the **Ajivika** sect — option **(3)**.
**Kharavela** followed **Jainism**; the **Ajivika** sect belongs to **Makkhali Gosala**.
**Amoghavarsha I** was a disciple of **Jinasena**; **Heliodorus** — **Bhagavata Religion**; **Gupta rulers** — **Vaishnavism** — all true.
xa: **Samprati** was a **patron** of Jainism.
**Bhadrabahu**'s followers = **Digambar**; **Sthulabhadra**'s followers = **Shwetambara**.
**Matsyendranath**'s followers = **Nathpanth**.

49.s: Who founded the Pashupata sect?
49.x: The Pashupata sect of Shaivism traces its foundation to Lakulisha.

49.s: Who was the founder of the Ajivika sect?
49.x: The Ajivika sect, which believed in determinism, was founded by Makkhali Gosala.

49.s: Which of the following continued despite the Bhakti and Sufi movements?
49.x: The movements did not end purdah or restrictions on women's public life, and caste inequalities persisted.
xa: Medieval norms grew **more restrictive** for women and lower castes: purdah, limited education and work.
Yet women like **Mirabai, Andal, Lal Ded** found room for open spiritual expression.

49.s: What was a limitation of Srivaishnavism and Veerashaivism?
o: They made caste inequality their principal objective
They had no concern with social reform
They ended every form of social discrimination
They opposed caste, but caste inequalities could not be eradicated
49.x: Although Srivaishnavism and Veerashaivism sought to reduce caste differences, caste inequalities persisted.

49.s:
Consider the following statements about the limitations of the Bhakti and Sufi movements:
1. Caste persisted.
2. Purdah continued.
3. The sects remained free of sectarian hardening.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
49.x: Caste persisted and purdah stayed, but the sects hardened over time, so statement 3 is false.

52.s: By what name is the 1717 farman of Farrukhsiyar popularly known?
52.x: The 1717 farman granted important trading privileges to the Company and is popularly called the Magna Carta of the Company.
52.tq: Recall the distinctive title associated with the 1717 farman.
xs: The **1717 farman** of **Farrukhsiyar** is called the **"Magna Carta" of the Company** — option **(3)**.
It gave **duty-free trade** in Bengal for **Rs 3,000** a year.
xa: **Diwani** = **revenue + civil justice** — a later grant (**1765**), not the farman.
**Dastak** misuse caused quarrels with **Siraj** and later **Mir Qasim**.

52.s: What was a dastak under the Bengal trading system?
o: land grant issued to a zamindar
permit for fortifying a European settlement
military order issued by the Nawab
52.x: A dastak was a free pass that enabled duty-free trade. Its misuse became a major source of conflict between the Company and the Nawabs.
52.tq: Test the precise meaning of a confusable administrative term.
xs: A **dastak** was a **free pass for duty-free trade** — option **(4)**.
**Company servants misused dastaks** for **private trade**, draining the Nawab's revenue.
xa: Dastak misuse caused quarrels with **Siraj** and later **Mir Qasim**.
**Mir Qasim** **abolished all internal trade duties**, so the dastak advantage vanished.

52.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Diwani granted to the East India Company?
o: The right to collect revenue and administer civil justice in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
The right to appoint the Mughal Emperor and control Delhi
The right to conduct foreign affairs on behalf of Awadh
The right to administer criminal justice and maintain the police in Bengal alone
52.x: Diwani comprised revenue collection and civil justice in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
52.tq: Discriminate between Diwani functions and the Nizamat functions retained by the Nawab.
xs: **Diwani** = **revenue collection and civil justice** in **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa** — option **(1)**.
**Criminal justice and police** form the **Nizamat**, kept by the Nawab.
xa: Granted by **Shah Alam II** under the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**.
**Naib diwans**: **Muhammad Reza Khan** (Bengal) + **Raja Shitab Rai** (Bihar).

52.s: Under the Dual Government in Bengal, criticised as "power without responsibility", which of the following did the Nawab formally retain?
52.x: The Company enjoyed the financial power of the Diwani, while the Nawab formally retained the Nizamat and its responsibilities.

52.s: For what fixed annual payment could the Company trade in Bengal without customs duties under the farman of 1717?
52.x: Farrukhsiyar's farman let the Company trade duty-free in Bengal for a fixed Rs 3,000 a year.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s: Who issued the farman of 1717 granting the Company duty-free trade in Bengal?
52.x: The 1717 farman, the "Magna Carta" of the Company, was issued by Farrukhsiyar.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s: What did the term 'Nizamat' mean in the administration of Bengal?
o: Police, criminal justice and law and order
52.x: Nizamat meant police, criminal justice and law and order; Diwani meant revenue and civil justice.

52.s: Who was the Nawab of Bengal when the Battle of Buxar was fought?
52.x: On 22/23 October, 1764 A.D. British Army defeated allied forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Oudh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. British Army’s command was in the hands of Major Hector Munro in the Battle of Buxar. The battle of Buxar assured the result of Plassey battle and established British supremacy on Banaras and Allahabad (Prayagraj) across the Ganges. The battle of Buxar made way for British and proved that there was no strong competitor before the British. The battle of Buxar completed what Plassey had begun. During the battle of Buxar Nawab of Bengal was Mir Jafar. According to Sir James Stephen, ‘’The battle of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as the origin of British power in India”. If the results of both significant battles are analyzed, it can be said that the battle of Plassey was won by treachery, but the battle of Buxar showed the supremacy of English armies and military skills. Plassey made the English the only controllers of Bengal while Buxar raised the political prestige of the Company throughout India.

52.s: Whose son was Najm-ud-Daula, who became Nawab of Bengal in 1765?
52.x: Najm-ud-Daula was Mir Jafar's son; he held the Nizamat in name only.
xa: **Diwani** = revenue + civil justice; **Nizamat** = police, criminal justice.
**Dual Government** lasted **1765-72**; **Warren Hastings** ended it.
**Raja Shitab Rai** was naib diwan for **Bihar**.

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Siraj-ud-Daulah – Killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari
Sarfaraz Khan – Stopped both companies fortifying Calcutta and Chandannagar
Alivardi Khan – Killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari
52.x: Siraj-ud-Daulah killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari; Sarfaraz Khan was killed by Alivardi, who stopped the fortifications.
xa: **Murshid Quli Khan** = last Subahdar appointed by the Mughal emperor (**UPPSC 2021**).
**Siraj-ud-Daulah** was **Alivardi's grandson**.

52.s: To which Naib Subahdar were defence and administration handed under Najm-ud-Daula (1765)?
52.x: The 1765 arrangement handed defence and administration to the Naib Subahdar Muhammad Reza Khan; the Nawab kept the Nizamat in name only.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s:
Which of the following is the correct sequence of these Nawabs of Bengal?
1. Mir Qasim
2. Alivardi Khan
3. Mir Jafar
4. Siraj-ud-Daulah
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
52.x: Alivardi Khan (1740–56) was followed by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah (1756–57), then Mir Jafar (1757–60) and Mir Qasim (1760–63).

52.s: The Mulki rule agitation took place during the rule of

Consider the following statements

A. Black hole incident occurred on 20th June, 1747

B. The Battle of Plassey paved the way for the British mastery of Bengal

C. The Battle of Plassey Marked the beginning of drain of wealth from India to Britain
Identify the correct statement(s) from the above.
Which of the following Indian rulers took the side of British during the war of 1857 and fought with Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi?
The battlefield of Plassey is situated in –
52.x: Plassey (present name - Palasi) battlefield is located on the banks of the Bhagirathi River in Nadia district of West Bengal. On 23 June 1757 AD, the troops of the British East India Company led by Robert Clive defeated Nawab of Bengal Sirajuddaula, in the historic Battle of Plassey.

52.s: Following the Battle of Plassey, which one of the following combinations of concessions was obtained by the Company?
o: Kora and Allahabad, together with the Nizamat of Bengal
Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and control of Awadh
The whole of Bengal without the appointment of a Nawab
Zamindari of the 24 Parganas, duty-free trade and resources to fight the French
52.x: After Plassey, the Company obtained the zamindari of the 24 Parganas, duty-free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and resources to fight the French.
52.tq: Group the immediate commercial, territorial and strategic results of one event.
xs: After Plassey the Company got the **zamindari of the 24 Parganas**, **duty-free trade** in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, and **resources to beat the French** — option **(4)**.
**Diwani** and **Awadh's** dependence came after **Buxar**; **Kora and Allahabad** went to **Shah Alam II** in **1765**.
xa: Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid **Rs 1.77 crore**.
Plassey: **puppet Nawab, 24 Parganas**; Buxar: **Diwani**, Awadh dependent.

52.s: Who was the last independent Nawab of Bengal?
52.x: Siraj-ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab, was defeated by Clive at Plassey despite French support.
xa: Conspirators inside his army: **Mir Jafar**, **Rai Durlabh**, **Jagat Seth**, **Omichund**, **Manik Chand**.
Loyal: **Mir Madan** + **Mohan Lal**.

52.s: Which of the following was NOT a cause of conflict between the English Company and Siraj-ud-Daulah?
o: Fortification of Calcutta without the Nawab's consent
Misuse of dastaks by Company servants
Sheltering of the Nawab's enemies by the Company
French refusal to obey the Nawab's order to stop fortification
52.x: The French obeyed the order to stop fortification; it was the English who continued fortifying Calcutta.
xa: **Black Hole (June 1756)**: Siraj took **Qasim Bazar** → **Calcutta (Fort William)**.
Governor **Drake** fled to **Fulta**.

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the conspiracy surrounding the Battle of Plassey?
o: Mir Madan — principal conspirator against Siraj
Governor Drake — leader of the anti-Company faction
52.x: Mir Jafar, who held the office of Mir Bakshi, was a principal conspirator against Siraj-ud-Daulah. Mir Madan was loyal to Siraj, while Holwell and Drake were associated with the British side.
52.tq: Use the person-office relationship to eliminate swapped roles.
xs: **Mir Jafar — Mir Bakshi** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Mir Madan** was **loyal** to Siraj, not a conspirator.
**Holwell** was a European prisoner in the Black Hole; **Drake** was the Governor who fled to **Fulta**.
xa: Other conspirators: **Rai Durlabh**, **Jagat Seth**, **Amir Chand (Omichund)**, **Manik Chand**.
Mir Jafar paid **Rs 1.77 crore** on becoming Nawab.

52.s: Which one of the following was a consequence specifically associated with the Battle of Buxar rather than the Battle of Plassey?
o: The Company restored the privileges of the 1717 farman.
The Company obtained the zamindari of the 24 Parganas.
Mir Jafar became Nawab of Bengal.
The Company secured the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and made Awadh dependent.
52.x: Buxar led to the grant of Diwani over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and reduced Awadh to a dependent position. The other consequences relate to Plassey or the Treaty of Alinagar.
52.tq: Separate the consequences of two closely connected events.
xs: **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa** and a **dependent Awadh** came from **Buxar** — option **(4)**.
**1717 farman privileges** were restored at **Alinagar (Feb 1757)**.
**24 Parganas** and **Mir Jafar as Nawab** were results of **Plassey**.
xa: Buxar's enemy: **Bengal + Awadh + Mughal Emperor** together.
Plassey's result: **puppet Nawab**, **24 Parganas**.

52.s: The Battle of Plassey was fought on which of the following dates and at which place?
52.x: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 at Palashi, also known as Plassey, on the Bhagirathi River.
52.tq: Use the date-place combination to distinguish closely related battles.
xs: Plassey: **23 June 1757**, at **Plassey (Palashi)** — option **(3)**.
It lay on the **Bhagirathi**, in **Nadia** district, **West Bengal**.
**22 October 1764** is **Buxar**, fought in Bihar.
xa: **Clive** (about **3,000**) defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah** (about **50,000**).
**23 June 2026** = **269th** anniversary of Plassey.

52.s: Which one of the following was NOT a conspirator against Siraj-ud-Daula at Plassey?
52.x: Mir Madan was loyal to Siraj-ud-Daula and was not among the conspirators. Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh and Jagat Seth were associated with the conspiracy.
52.tq: Find the loyal commander hidden among the names of the conspirators.
xs: **Mir Madan** was **loyal to Siraj** — not a conspirator — option **(1)**.
Conspirators: **Mir Jafar** (Mir Bakshi), **Rai Durlabh**, **Jagat Seth**, **Amir Chand (Omichund)**, **Manik Chand**.
xa: **Mohan Lal** was also loyal to Siraj.
⚠ Trap: listing **Mir Madan** among the traitors is WRONG (**Jul 2026** practice question).

52.s: The Plassey battlefield lies in which district of West Bengal?
52.x: Palashi, on the Bhagirathi, is in Nadia district, West Bengal.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s: After the Battle of Plassey, in which provinces did the Company get the right of duty-free trade?
52.x: Mir Jafar gave the Company duty-free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, along with the zamindari of the 24 Parganas.

52.s: Which of the following correctly represents the two periods of Mir Jafar's tenure as Nawab of Bengal?
52.x: Mir Jafar served as Nawab from 1757 to 1760 and again from 1763 to 1765, after the fall of Mir Qasim.
52.tq: Test the two-tenure pattern instead of treating the office as a single continuous term.
xs: Mir Jafar ruled **1757-1760** and again **1763-1765** — option **(4)**.
**1760-63** was **Mir Qasim**; **1756-57** was **Siraj-ud-Daulah**.
xa: First term: after Plassey; removed in **1760** — could not meet Company demands.
Second term: restored after **Mir Qasim's fall**; accepted **limits on his army**; died soon after **Buxar**.

52.s: Mir Jafar's intrigue with which European power led to the Company's victory at Chinsura or Bidara in 1759?
52.x: Mir Jafar plotted with the Dutch against the English, but Clive defeated the Dutch at Chinsura or Bidara in 1759, after which the Dutch left India.
52.tq: Match the Indian political actor with the European ally involved in the intrigue.
xs: Mir Jafar plotted with the **Dutch**; Clive beat them at **Chinsura/Bidara (1759)** — option **(4)**.
After this the **Dutch left India**.
xa: Mir Jafar was removed in **1760** — he could not meet **Company demands**.
Pension: **Rs 15,000 a month** (some notes print "Rs 1,500 annually").

52.s: Which one of the following was a reason for Mir Jafar's removal from office in 1760?
o: He surrendered Bengal to the Dutch.
He refused to accept the grant of Diwani to the Company.
He could not meet the Company's demands.
52.x: Mir Jafar was removed in 1760 because he could not meet the increasing demands of the Company.
52.tq: Identify the stated cause rather than a later consequence of his rule.
xs: Mir Jafar was removed in **1760** because he **could not meet the Company's demands** — option **(4)**.
He was a **conspirator** against Siraj at Plassey, not a supporter; **Diwani** was granted only in **1765**.
xa: He got a pension of **Rs 15,000 a month**.
**Vansittart** put **Mir Qasim**, his son-in-law, on the throne in **1760**.

52.s: What sum did Mir Jafar pay the Company after Plassey?
52.x: Mir Jafar paid Rs 1.77 crore and gave the Company the zamindari of the 24 Parganas.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Mir Jafar was the Nawab of Bengal when the Battle of Buxar was fought.
2. Mir Qasim fought at Buxar as the reigning Nawab of Bengal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
52.x: Mir Jafar had been restored as Nawab in 1763 and held the post during Buxar; Mir Qasim fought there as the ex-Nawab.

52.s: Out of the below mentioned Nawabs, who tried to raise a modern and discipline Army on European lines?
Which of these Nawabs of Bengal abolished all duties on internal trade?
Which of the following shifted his capital from Murshidabad to Munger?
52.x: Mir Qasim was the most efficient successor among the successors of Nawab Alivardi Khan. He demonstrated his capability as Fauzdar of Poornia and Rangpur. He transferred his capital from Murshidabad to Munger. The reason was to secure himself from constant interference from Calcutta and intrigues of Murshidabad. He organized his Army on the European model. He managed the factory of arms and ammunition at Munger for manufacturing of tanks and matchlock guns. Besides, Mir Qasim had made efforts to reform state’s financial condition.

52.s: Which of these Nawabs of Bengal abolished all duties on internal trade?
52.x: Mir Qasim abolished all duties on internal trade in 1763, which angered the English East India Company.

52.s: Who placed Mir Qasim on the throne of Bengal in 1760?
52.x: Mir Qasim, the son-in-law of Mir Jafar, was placed on the throne in 1760 by Governor Vansittart.
52.tq: Use the ruler–appointing authority pair rather than confusing the successive Governors of Bengal.
xs: **Governor Vansittart** put **Mir Qasim** on the throne in **1760** — option **(1)**.
Mir Qasim was **Mir Jafar's son-in-law**.
**Warren Hastings** came in **1772**; **Clive** returned in **May 1765**.
xa: **Treaty of 1760**: ceded **Burdwan, Midnapur and Chittagong**.
He moved the capital **Murshidabad to Monghyr (Munger), Bihar**.

52.s: Why did the abolition of internal trade duties by Mir Qasim lead to conflict with the Company’s servants?
o: It prevented Indian merchants from trading outside Bengal.
It made Indian merchants compete on equal terms with English merchants and removed the advantage derived from dastaks.
It transferred the Company’s Diwani rights to the Nawab.
It imposed a new uniform duty exclusively on English merchants.
52.x: By abolishing internal duties, Mir Qasim placed Indian merchants on an equal footing with English merchants and removed the advantage that Company servants obtained through misuse of dastaks.
52.tq: Trace the economic consequence of equal trade treatment to identify the cause of the conflict.
xs: Abolishing internal duties made **Indian merchants pay the same as the English**, ending the **dastak** advantage — option **(2)**.
**Company servants**, angry at lost **private-trade profits**, went to war.
xa: Asked in **APPSC G2 2017**.
Mir Qasim was **defeated in 1763** and fled to **Awadh**.

52.s: Which Nawab of Bengal shifted his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr and abolished all internal trade duties?
52.x: Mir Qasim (1760-63) moved the capital to Monghyr (Munger) in Bihar and abolished all inland duties, so Indian merchants paid the same as the English. Mir Jafar was the puppet after Plassey, Siraj lost Plassey, and Najm-ud-Daula was Nawab from 1765 in name only.
52.tq: Mir Qasim = Monghyr + abolished internal duties (APPSC G2 2017)
xs: **Mir Qasim** moved the capital to **Monghyr (Munger)** and **abolished all internal trade duties** — option **(2)**.
**Mir Jafar** was a **puppet**; **Siraj** lost Plassey; **Najm-ud-Daula** kept the **Nizamat** in name only from **1765**.
xa: He also **modernised the army**.
He was **Mir Jafar's son-in-law**.

52.s: The immediate result of the Company’s conflict with Mir Qasim in 1763 was that he
o: was restored to the throne of Bengal
surrendered directly to Shah Alam II at Delhi
fled to Awadh after being defeated
joined the British and became Governor of Bengal
52.x: The Company defeated Mir Qasim in 1763, after which he fled to Awadh and later became one of the allies against the British at Buxar.
52.tq: Link the defeat year with the correct subsequent movement of the defeated ruler.
xs: Mir Qasim was **defeated in 1763** and **fled to Awadh** — option **(3)**.
**Mir Jafar**, not Mir Qasim, was **restored** in **1763**.
xa: At **Buxar (1764)** he fought as the **deposed Nawab of Bengal** alongside **Shuja-ud-Daulah** and **Shah Alam II**.
Mir Qasim ruled **1760-63**.

52.s: Of which areas was Mir Qasim the Fauzdar before he became Nawab?
52.x: Mir Qasim, son-in-law of Mir Jafar, was earlier Fauzdar of Purnia and Rangpur.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s: Whose son-in-law was Mir Qasim, who became Nawab of Bengal in 1760?
52.x: Mir Qasim was the son-in-law of Mir Jafar; Governor Vansittart placed him on the throne in 1760.

52.s: Where did Mir Qasim set up a gun factory to arm his army trained on European lines?

52.s: Which one of the following rulers had granted Diwani to the East India Company?
52.x: As per the first Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765 A.D.), the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the Company’s protection and was to reside at Allahabad. The Emperor issued an order dated 12th August, 1765 granting Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. During this time Robert Clive was Governor of East India Company in Bengal. The emperor’s order legalized the political authority of Company in Bengal and British rule expanded all over India including Delhi. Successors of Shah Alam II i.e. Akbar II (1806-37 A.D.) and Bahadurshah II (1837-57 A.D.) became pensioners of East India Company.

52.s: Who was appointed Deputy Diwan of Murshidabad by Robert Clive after the Allahabad Treaty?
52.x: According to the Treaty of Allahabad (August, 1765 A.D.), Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the Company’s protection and had to reside at Allahabad. Shah Alam II conferred Diwani (fiscal revenue collection authority) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company by issuing ‘Farman’ on 12 August, 1765 A.D. Nazm-ud-duala (son of Mir Jafar) was accepted as Nawab of Bengal. In return, the company had to pay the emperor an annual sum of Rs 26 Lakhs as pension. At that time, the Company was neither interested in taking responsibility for tax revenue collection nor was it capable of doing so. Therefore, the Company appointed two Diwans- Mohammad Raza Khan for Bengal and Raja Shitab Rai for Bihar. Thus, all business of Diwani and Nizamat was conducted by Indians but authorized by the British Company.

54.s: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
o: To maintain a large standing army at others expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
54.x: Statement (c) does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance: The primary objective was to establish military and political dominance rather than ensuring a stable revenue for the Company. Though the Subsidiary Alliance system was quite old, Wellesley gave it a definite shape. Under the system, the ruler of the allied Indian state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. The ruler, unable to pay the expenses, had to cede a part of his kingdom to the British. The British agreed to defend the ruler from his enemies. They also controlled the defence and foreign relations of the protected ally. In return, the Indian ruler of the protected state should keep a British Resident at his court and disband his own army.  Indian rulers should not employ Europeans in their service without the approval of the British.  Indian rulers should not negotiate with any other Indian ruler without consulting the Governor-General. • The System of Subsidiary Alliance was also aimed at preventing French influence (the Napoleonic threat) from entering India. This system enabled the British to uphold a substantial army, with the financial burden falling Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 154 on the local rulers (it helped the British to have paramountcy over the Indian States), and was not implemented for securing a fixed income for the East India Company.

54.x: Governor-General Lord Wellesley came to India in 1798 A.D. at a time when the British were locked in a life and death struggle with France all over the world. The fear of Napoleon haunted the Britishers everywhere. To achieve his political aims, Wellesley relied on the system of Subsidiary Alliance. While the practice of helping Indian rulers with a paid British force was quite old, it was given shape by Wellesley who used it to sub-ordinate the Indian states to the paramountcy of the company. Under the subsidiary Alliance system, the ruler of the allying state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. However, to secure a fixed income for the company was not under the agenda of the Subsidiary Alliance.

101.s:
Statement (A): Moturpha is a salt tax levied by the British East India Company.
Statement (B): The revenue collected by the British East India Company from the Zamindars is called Peshcush.
101.x:
Statement (A) is false. Moturpha was not a salt tax. It was a professional or trade tax imposed on artisans, craftsmen, traders and occupational groups by the British East India Company. The salt tax was a separate levy imposed on the manufacture and sale of salt.
Statement (B) is true. Peshcush refers to the fixed annual tribute or land revenue paid by Zamindars to the British East India Company under the Zamindari system. It became an important source of revenue during British rule in the Madras Presidency. Therefore, Statement (A) is false and Statement (B) is true. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Moturpha – Tax on professions, trades and occupations.
• Peshcush – Fixed revenue paid by Zamindars to the British.

53.x: Marathas opposed the British vigorously in India. Maratha were suppressed after three Anglo-Maratha Wars. On the ruins of Mughal Empire, Maratha laid down their foundation and British also took advantage of these circumstances. British lost first Anglo-Maratha war badly and this war ended with the Treaty of Salbai. Lord Wellesley trapped Peshwa in the cage of Subsidiary Alliance in 1802. Regional States : Punjab and Mysore *Ranjit Singh was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on 13 th November, 1780 A.D. Treaty of Amritsar was signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and British East India Company on 25 th April, 1809 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured Multan in 1818 A.D., Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D.. *In 1798 AD, Zaman Shah attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799 A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of Lahore and made it his Capital. Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (in return of his service and providing tanks and artileries) and appointed him as the Subedar of Lahore. He also captured Amritsar from Bhangi Misl in 1802

53.s: Subsidiary Alliance was implemented during the reign of –
53.x: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) cleverly used a subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First Subsidiary Alliance was signed in 1765 with Awadh where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Awadh on a fixed payment to the Company. The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 AD and 1800 AD), Mysore (1799 AD), Tanjore (1799 AD), Oudh (1801 AD), Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle of Barar (1803 AD), Sindhiya (1804 AD), Holkar (1818 AD), Jodhpur, Jaipur, Machheri, Bundi and Bharatpur. Note : Hyderabad will be the answer if it is asked first state to join Wellesley's subsidiary alliance.

60.s: Out of the following, which was the "Munro system" developed by Thomas Munro?
Who was mainly responsible for introducing the Ryotwari System in the Madras Presidency?
60.x:
The Ryotwari System was introduced in the Madras Presidency by Sir Thomas Munro during the early nineteenth century. Under this system, the government collected land revenue directly from individual cultivators (Ryots) instead of through Zamindars or intermediaries. Every ryot was recognized as the proprietor of his land, provided he regularly paid the land revenue fixed by the government. The system was first experimented with in parts of South India and later became the principal land revenue system in the Madras Presidency. It aimed to eliminate intermediaries, but in practice the heavy land tax often placed a severe burden on cultivators. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Ryotwari System → Sir Thomas Munro
• Direct settlement between Government and Ryot
• Introduced mainly in Madras Presidency

60.x: Ryotwari System was the second system of collection of land revenue after Permanent Settlement. Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read were the founders of this system. 60.s: Sir Thomas Munro is associated with the land revenue settlement:
60.x: Ryotwari System was the second system of collection of land revenue after Permanent Settlement. Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read were the founders of this system. In Ryotwari System, the ownership rights were transferred to the peasants. British government collected taxes directly from the peasants around 51% of British occupied Indian area was included in this system. The high rate of taxes and strictness during collection became a significant cause of struggle between money lenders and peasants.

61.x: The constant flow of wealth from India to England for which India did not get an adequate economic, commercial or material return has been described by national leaders and economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from India. Before 1813 company had a recurring surplus which accrued from (a) profits from oppressive land revenue policy (b) profits from its trade resulting from monopolistic control over Indian markets and exactions (c) made by the company’s officials. All this surplus was used by the Company as an “investment”, i.e. for making a purchase of exportable items in India and elsewhere. Against the exports of goods made out of this investment, India did not get anything in return. This system was brought to an end by the charter act of 1813. From 1813 onwards economic drain took the form of ‘unrequited’ exports. Barring a few exceptional years, a favourable balance of trade had been the normal feature of our foreign trade till the outbreak of world war II. Therefore, it is clear that (A) and (R) both are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). Dadabhai Naoroji described the drain of wealth as the “evil of all evils” and the leading cause of Indian poverty.

61.x: In India, traditional livelihoods, especially those of weavers and artisans, suffered severely under British policies, yet this did not coincide with the emergence of indigenous industries. Instead, the British East India Company's monopolistic control and exploitative practices systematically dismantled India's traditional economic structure, leading to deindustrialisation. The Company flooded the Indian market with cheap, machine-made textiles from England, undermining local crafts and forcing Indian artisans out of work. Furthermore, high tariffs and restrictive policies prevented Indian industries from flourishing, thereby stifling any potential industrial growth. The combination of the suppression of local industries and the lack of protective policies for Indian artisans created a vacuum that the local economy could not fill. This stark economic divergence between industrialising Europe and a deindustrialising India deepened the economic disparities between the two regions, illustrating the profoundly destructive impact of British colonial policies on India's economy.

61.x: The triangular trade between India, China, and England in the 18th and 19th centuries was centered on opium. The British East India Company established their monopoly in the cultivation of opium in the region of Bengal and Bihar etc., they forced the farmers to cultivate opium and exported it to China, where it was in high demand despite government bans. Profits from the opium trade were used to purchase Chinese goods like tea, silk, and porcelain for England, while manufactured goods from England were exported to India, completing the trade cycle. This exploitative system had severe social and economic consequences, including the Opium Wars between Britain and China. While commodities like silk and black pepper were also traded, opium was the chief economic foundation of this triangular commerce.

61.s: The artificially fixed rupee-sterling exchange rate prescribed by the Hilton-Young Commission (1926) was adopted by the British Government for which one of the following reasons?
o: Aiding the flow of remittances from India and maintaining India's creditworthiness
Encouraging the export of cotton produce from India
Preventing depreciation of the Rupee in terms of gold
61.x: Statement (a) is the correct answer: The Hilton-Young Commission recommended fixing the rupee-sterling exchange rate at 1s. 6d. (one rupee = 1 shilling and 6 pence). This was an artificially high (overvalued) rate compared to what many Indian nationalists and economists demanded (1s. 4d.). The British Government adopted this rate to facilitate the smooth and cheaper transfer of remittances from India to Britain. These included pensions of British officials, interest on public debt, military expenses, and dividends of British companies. A stronger rupee meant fewer rupees were needed to buy the required sterling for these remittances. It helped maintain India's creditworthiness in the London money market, making it easier for the Government of India to raise loans in Britain. Statement (b) is incorrect: An overvalued rupee made imported British goods cheaper for Indian buyers, benefiting British manufacturers and hurting Indian industries, which faced stiff competition from cheaper imports. Indian importers benefited, but this was not the main British motive. Statement (c) is incorrect: The artificially fixed high exchange rate hurt Indian exports (including cotton). Statement (d) is incorrect: The rate was fixed in relation to sterling, not primarily to prevent depreciation against gold. • Note: The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) has recently been in the news because 2026 marks the 100 th anniversary of its recommendations, which ultimately paved the way for the establishment

56.s: With reference to the ‘revolt of 1857’ who of the following was betrayed by ‘friend’ captured and put to death by the British?

He progressed with the Gwalior contingent after the British reoccupation of Kanpur and forced Lieutenant General Charles Ash Windham to retreat from Kanpur. Later on, he came to the rescue of Rani Lakshmibai. However, he was defeated by General Napier's troops and was executed by the British Government (after he was captured in the forest of Paron due to betrayal of his friend Mansingh) at Shivpuri on 18th April 1859. One of the greatest heroes of the Great Uprising of 1857, Tatya Tope was born in 1814 at Yeola in Maharashtra. He was the only child of Pandurang and his wife, Rukhmabai. Having been brought up in Bithoor, he came into contact with Nana Saheb Peshwa. He was a great admirer of Nana Saheb and was ready to sacrifice his life for him. 102.s: Battle of Padmanabha (1794) decided whose defeat?
o: The ruler of Vizianagaram, Vijayarama Raju
102.x:
The Battle of Padmanabham, fought on 10 July 1794, was a decisive conflict between the British East India Company and the Vizianagaram ruler, Pusapati Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II. The conflict arose over the Company's growing interference in the affairs of the Vizianagaram estate and disputes relating to tribute payments. Refusing to accept British domination, Vijayarama Raju confronted the Company's forces at Padmanabham. The battle ended in a decisive British victory, and Vijayarama Raju was killed. This marked the decline of the political power of the Vizianagaram Zamindari and strengthened British control over the Northern Circars. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Year – 1794
• Place – Padmanabham
• Result – British victory and death of Vijayarama Raju

102.s:
Assertion (A): Andhra region was not greatly affected by the Revolt of 1857 as Andhra had no local leaders.
Reason (R): The then reigning Nizam, Nawab Afzal-ud-Dowla adopted a pro-British attitude.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
102.x:
Assertion (A) is false. It is incorrect to state that the Andhra region remained unaffected by the Revolt of 1857 because there were no local leaders. Although the revolt did not assume the same intensity as in North India, several local revolts and anti-British activities occurred in Andhra and the Hyderabad State. Leaders such as Turrebaz Khan in Hyderabad actively resisted the British, and anti-British sentiment was visible in different parts of the Telugu-speaking region. Therefore, the absence of local leaders was not the reason for the limited impact of the revolt.
Reason (R) is true. The Nizam of Hyderabad, Afzal-ud-Dowla (Asaf Jah V), remained loyal to the British during the Revolt of 1857. His cooperation helped the British suppress revolutionary activities in the Deccan and prevented the uprising from spreading widely in the Hyderabad State. The loyalty of the Nizam was one of the important reasons for the failure of the revolt in the Deccan. Since the Assertion is false and the Reason is true, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Nizam during 1857 – Afzal-ud-Dowla
• Hyderabad Resident – Played a key role in suppressing the revolt.

64.s: Who established the first Prarthana Samaj in Andhra in 1878?

Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu established the first Prarthana Samaj in Andhra at Rajahmundry in 1878. Inspired by the reform movements of western India, particularly the Brahmo Samaj and Prarthana Samaj, Veeresalingam used this organization to promote women's education, widow remarriage, opposition to child marriage and the eradication of social superstitions. The Prarthana Samaj became an important platform for spreading modern education and rational thinking among the Telugu-speaking people. Through this institution and his writings, Veeresalingam laid the foundation for the social reform movement in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

• Established – 1878
• Place – Rajahmundry
• Objective – Social and religious reforms

67.s: The Vital-Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by
67.x: Gopal Baba Walangkar was born in 1840 into a Mahar family near Mahad. An ex-army man, he was deeply influenced by Jyotirao Phule and adopted his ideas on social equality. Walangkar supported Phule's Aryan invasion theory and argued that the untouchables were the indigenous inhabitants of India, while the Brahmins were descendants of Aryans who had invaded the country. In 1886, Walangkar established the anti-caste organisation "Anarya Dosh-Parihar Samaj" to address the Dalit issues. In 1888, Walangkar started a monthly journal, Vital-Vidhvansak, which was the first to target the untouchables. He is credited with pioneering Dalit periodicals. Additional Information: In the 19 TH century, educated Indians started several journals. However, most of these were started by Brahmins and did not discuss the challenges faced by Dalits. This led to the emergence of Dalit periodicals, in which Dalits discussed their issues. Gopal Baba Walangkar, Shivram Janba Kamble, Kisan Fagu Bansode and Dr. Ambedkar played an important role in discussing Dalit issues in journals or periodicals. Founder/Editor Journal/Magazine Shivram Janba Kamble Somvanshiy Mitra (The friend of the depressed classes) Kisan Fagu Bansode Nirashrit Hind Nagarik, Vital Vidhwansak, Majur Patrika and Chokhamela Dr. B. 67.s: Who among the following was the founder of the 'Self-Respect Movement'?
67.x: The Self Respect Movement (SRM), founded in 1925 by E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar) in Tamil Nadu, was built on earlier Dravidian reform efforts. It aimed to secularise Tamizh society, promote rationalism, and challenge caste hierarchies, laying the foundation for modern Dravidian politics. The movement, called 'Suyamariyathai' or Self- Respect, symbolises the idea that 'Maanam' or honour is a basic human instinct that distinguishes humans from other animals. Periyar identified the notion of self-respect with three other important concepts: ' Samathuvam' (Equality), 'Suthanthiram' (Freedom) and 'Samadharmam' (Communism).

68.s: Who was the founder of the first girls' schools at Rajahmundry?
68.x:
Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu was one of the greatest social reformers in Andhra Pradesh and is widely regarded as the Father of the Telugu Renaissance. At a time when female education was neglected, Veeresalingam took the pioneering step of establishing the first girls' school at Rajahmundry in 1874. He firmly believed that education was essential for the empowerment of women and for the progress of society. Apart from promoting women's education, he campaigned vigorously for widow remarriage, opposed child marriage, and fought against social superstitions. Through his writings, journals and reform movements, he laid the foundation for modern social reform in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

This title recognizes Veeresalingam's pioneering contribution to modern social reform in Andhra Pradesh. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

68.x:
Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu was one of the foremost social reformers of Andhra Pradesh. He actively campaigned against the Bhogam (Devadasi) system, which subjected women to social exploitation. Through public awareness, education and social reform movements, he worked tirelessly for the rehabilitation and upliftment of women affected by the system. His efforts greatly contributed to the gradual abolition of the Bhogam practice in Andhra society. Apart from this, he also promoted women's education, moral reform and social equality. 68.s: The father of Movement for peoples dialect in Telugu Language was
Who founded the Varthamana Vyavaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samaj?
68.x:
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy founded the Varthamana Vyavaharika Andhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samaj to promote the use of spoken (Vyavaharika) Telugu instead of the highly Sanskritized classical language. He believed that education and literature should be written in a language easily understood by ordinary people. His movement revolutionized Telugu prose and greatly influenced modern Telugu literature, journalism and education. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Founder – Gidugu Ramamurthy
• Movement – Vyavaharika (Colloquial) Telugu

68.s: Who founded Vartamana Vyavaaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samajam?
Who wrote the "Savara manual" in English?
68.x: Gidugu Ramamurthy prepared a Savara grammar in English (1931) and a Savara-English dictionary (1936). He is known as the father of the Telugu vyavaharika language movement.

68.s: Who started the Vyavaharika Bhasha movement for Telugu language?
68.x: Gidugu Ramamurthy is known as the father of the Vyavaharika Bhasha movement.

68.s: Who inspired the Vyavaharika Telugu movement?
68.x: J. A. Yates inspired the movement for the use of Vyavaharika Telugu.
68.tq: Discriminate among the individuals associated with different roles in the language movement.
xs: **J.A. Yates** inspired the vyavaharika movement — option **(3)**.
**P.T. Srinivasa Ayyangar** wrote **Life or Death: A Plea for Vernaculars**.
**Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu** and **Kokkonda Venkataratnam** were **opponents**.
xa: Grammars for vyavaharika: **Malladi Suryanarayana Sastri** (Andhra Bhashanusasanam), **Vadlamudi Gopalakrishnayya** (Vyavaharika Bhasha Vyakaranam).
**Vajjala Venkateswarlu**: Aadhunikapramanikandhra Vyakaranam.
Leaders: **Gidugu** (theory, education), **Gurajada** (literature).

68.s: Gidugu Ramamurthy was born on 29 August 1863 at which place?
68.x: Gidugu Ramamurthy was born on 29 August 1863 at Ponduru in the Srikakulam region.
68.tq: Use the birthplace and date together to identify the correct personality detail.
xs: Gidugu was born on **29 Aug 1863** at **Ponduru (Srikakulam)** — option **(4)**.
**Parlakimidi** is where he worked as a **Telugu teacher**; he worked mostly from **Vizianagaram**.
xa: He died on **22 Jan 1940**.
**Visakhapatnam** hosted the **1910** meeting that led to his Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Samstha.
He made a script and a **Savara-Telugu dictionary** for the Savara language (Ganjam Agency).

68.s: Which of the following was NOT one of Gidugu Ramamurthy’s contributions to Savara studies?
o: Preparing a Savara-Telugu and Telugu-Savara dictionary
68.x: Gidugu created a script, prepared bilingual dictionaries and wrote *A Manual of Savara Language*. The Andhra Sahitya Parishad was associated with the classical side of the language debate.
68.tq: Separate the individual’s documented linguistic work from an association linked to the opposing camp.
xs: **Establishing the Andhra Sahitya Parishad** was not Gidugu's — option **(3)**; through it **Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu** led the **classical** side.
Gidugu's Savara work: a **script**, a **Savara-Telugu / Telugu-Savara dictionary** and **A Manual of Savara Language**.
xa: Savara is spoken in the **Ganjam Agency**.
Other works: **A Memorandum of Modern Telugu Prose**, Bala Kavi Saranyam.
**Sri Sri** called him "**our recent inspiration**".

68.s: By which title is Gidugu Ramamurthy known?
68.x: Gidugu was known as Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Pitamaha and Abhinava Vaganushasanudu and received Rao Saheb and Kaisar-e-Hind; Andhra Kesari is not his title.
xa: He was also **Rao Saheb**; Kaisar-e-Hind came in **1934**.
⚠ **Rao Saheb** = Gidugu; **Rao Bahadur** = Veeresalingam (**1893**) and Venkataratnam Naidu.
**Andhra Ratna** = **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya**.

68.s: The classical side in the Telugu language controversy was led through which organisation by Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu?
68.x: Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu led the classical side through the Andhra Sahitya Parishad.
68.tq: Match the leader with the organisation representing his position.
xs: **Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu** led the classical side through the **Andhra Sahitya Parishad** — option **(4)**.
The **Navya Sahitya Parishat** and **Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Samstha** backed **spoken** Telugu; the **Andhra Mahasabha** finally endorsed it.
xa: **Andhra Sahitya Parishad magazine** — Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu (correct pair, APPSC **2019**).
The other orthodox opponent: **Kokkonda Venkataratnam** (Andhra Bhasha Sanjeevini).
⚠ **Parishad** (classical) vs **Parishat** (Navya Sahitya, vyavaharika).

68.s: With whom was the Telugu journal Janavani associated?
68.x: Janavani was associated with Tapi Dharma Rao; the monthly Telugu (1919) with Gidugu and the Andhra Sahitya Parishad magazine with Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu.
xa: ⚠ Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu led the **classical (granthika)** side; Gidugu and Tapi Dharma Rao backed **vyavaharika**.
**Andhra Patrika** = **Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao** (PYQ **2019**).
Gidugu founded the **Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Samstha** (**1910**).

68.s: Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led a movement against which literary style in Telugu?
68.x: Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the movement for Vyavaharika Bhasha, opposing the Sanskritised grandhika style. He was allied with Gurajada Apparao.
68.tq: Distinguish the spoken-language movement from unrelated literary and religious styles.
xs: Gidugu led the **vyavaharika** movement against the **Sanskritised grandhika** style — option **(2)**.
Granthika = Sanskritised classical Telugu with **archaic grammar**, claimed as the only "pure" literary medium.
xa: Vyavaharika = spoken Telugu (also **Gramya / Janapada bhasha**).
His ally in literature: **Gurajada Apparao**.
Outcome: the **Andhra Mahasabha** endorsed colloquial Telugu for literature, education and administration.

68.s: Along with Gurajada Apparao, who led the Vyavaharika (spoken Telugu) movement?
68.x: Gidugu and Gurajada led the Vyavaharika cause to narrow the gap between written and spoken Telugu, while orthodox pandits backed Granthika.
xa: Opponents: **Kokkonda Venkataratnam**, **Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu** (Andhra Sahitya Parishad).
Supporters: **Tapi Dharma Rao**, **Navya Sahitya Parishat**.

xs: Veeresalingam is called **Andhra Rammohan Roy** (Raja Ram Mohan Roy of Andhra) — option **(4)**.
**Andhra Ratna** = **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya**; **Kavi Raju** = **Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary**.
